sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.summary: Introduces Chapter 2 on field exploration, testing, and instrumentation for geotechnical investigations. Covers the full scope of the chapter including geologic maps, remote sensing, geophysical methods, borings, penetration tests, drilling and sampling, groundwater measurement, in situ testing, and field instrumentation selection.
key_points: Chapter covers exploration methods: geologic maps, air photos, remote sensing, geophysical methods, test borings/pits, and penetration resistance tests.
Also addresses drilling and sampling methods, groundwater measurements, in situ soil/rock properties, and field instrumentation selection.
Effective field investigation begins with a thorough assessment of project data needs before mobilization.
Three distinct phases of project exploration: reconnaissance/feasibility, preliminary, and detailed/final; a fourth phase may occur during/after construction.
Individual test borings should be supplemented by lower-cost techniques (test pits, probes, geophysical surveys), especially for remote or large-footprint projects.
For small projects, the three exploration phases are frequently combined into a single effort.
sections.applicability: Applies as an introductory overview whenever planning or executing a geotechnical field investigation program.

sections.title: Scope
sections.summary: Defines the scope of Chapter 2, enumerating the specific topics addressed: exploration methods (geologic maps, air photos, remote sensing), geophysical methods, test borings and pits, penetration resistance tests, drilling and sampling, groundwater measurements, in situ soil and rock property measurement, and selection of field instrumentation and geotechnical performance monitoring equipment.
sections.body: This chapter contains information on exploration methods including use of geologic maps, air photos, and remote sensing; geophysical methods; test borings and test pits, and penetration resistance tests. Also presented is information on methods of drilling and sampling, obtaining groundwater measurements, measuring in situ properties of soil and rock, selecting field instrumentation and geotechnical performance monitoring equipment.
key_points: Scope includes geologic maps, air photos, and remote sensing as primary reconnaissance tools.
Covers geophysical methods as a complement to direct sampling and testing.
Addresses test borings, test pits, and penetration resistance tests for subsurface characterization.
Includes drilling and sampling methods, groundwater measurement, and in situ soil/rock property testing.
Field instrumentation and geotechnical performance monitoring equipment selection is also addressed.
sections.applicability: Applies when determining what geotechnical exploration and testing topics are covered in Chapter 2 of UFC 3-220-10.

sections.title: Planning for Field Investigations
sections.summary: Describes best practices for planning geotechnical field investigations, including pre-mobilization research, use of existing data and geological reviews, desk-top studies with aerial photography and remote sensing, and the three (or four) phases of project exploration. Emphasizes supplementing borings with lower-cost methods and tailoring investigation scope to project data needs.
sections.body:
The initial phase of field investigations should commence with a thoughtful assessment of the data needs for the specific project, which will help define the objectives of the subsequent field investigation. Prior to mobilizing to the field, readily available information should be located that is relatively inexpensive and often invaluable. In cases where the new project is adjacent to an existing project (e.g., highway widening, lateral expansion of an existing levee, etc.), the initial research should focus on information and data that have previously been collected and/or compiled for the project. For a new project, the initial effort should include a detailed review of geological conditions at the site and within the region where the site is located. This should then be followed by a "desk top" study, utilizing sources of available data, including historical and current aerial photography, remote sensing imagery, and (whenever possible) a field reconnaissance. The collective information obtained from these activities should be used as a guide in planning the project-specific field exploration.

To the extent possible as dictated by project data needs, individual test borings should be supplemented by lower cost exploration techniques that include test pits, test probes, and geophysical surveys. This is particularly true for remote sites, sites exhibiting wide variability in subsurface conditions, projects occupying a large footprint, linear projects (e.g., roadways, pipelines, etc.), and projects in the offshore environment where mobilizations and test borings can be exceptionally expensive.

Project explorations generally have three distinct phases: (1) reconnaissance/feasibility exploration; (2) preliminary exploration; and (3) detailed/final exploration. These phases usually have different objectives. A fourth phase of exploration that involves additional sampling and/or in situ testing may be desired and/or required during or after construction to confirm conditions. Frequently (and most common for relatively small projects), these three phases are combined into a single exploration effort.

Reconnaissance includes a review of available topographic, geologic, and hydrogeologic information; aerial photographs; data from previous investigations and projects; and a site visit. Geophysical methods may prove to be helpful in many cases, particularly for large projects where subsurface conditions are variable and for linear projects (e.g., levees, highways, etc.). Reconnaissance/feasibility exploration frequently reveals difficulties which may be expected in later exploration phases and assists in determining the type, number and locations of borings required. Examples of information that can be obtained from field reconnaissance activities are presented in Table 2-1.
key_points: Begin with assessment of project data needs to define field investigation objectives before mobilization.
For projects adjacent to existing infrastructure, prioritize previously collected data; for new projects, start with a geological review and desk-top study.
Supplement test borings with lower-cost methods (test pits, probes, geophysical surveys), especially at remote, variable, large-footprint, linear, or offshore sites.
Three standard exploration phases: (1) reconnaissance/feasibility, (2) preliminary, (3) detailed/final; a fourth post-construction phase may also be needed.
For small projects, all three phases are commonly combined into one effort.
Reconnaissance/feasibility exploration reveals anticipated difficulties and guides type, number, and location of borings.
Table 2-1 provides examples of items evaluated during field reconnaissance, including access, utilities, surface soils, drainage, terrain, and past investigations.
sections.applicability: Applies when planning a geotechnical field investigation program for any project type, from initial scoping through final exploration phase design.

sections.title: PUBLISHED REFERENCE MATERIALS
sections.summary: Introduces the first step of a geotechnical investigation: identifying readily available and pertinent information from two primary sources — previous investigations and published literature in the public domain. Sets the context for subsections covering each source type and their role in reconnaissance.
sections.body: When starting an investigation, the first step is to identify sources of readily available and pertinent information. In general, this information comes from two sources: (1) previous investigations; and (2) published literature in the public domain.
key_points: The first step in any geotechnical investigation is to gather existing, readily available information before conducting new fieldwork.
Two primary information sources exist: previous investigations and published literature in the public domain.
Leveraging existing data reduces cost and accelerates the project team's understanding of site conditions.
sections.applicability: Applies when initiating a geotechnical site investigation and determining what background information should be gathered before fieldwork begins.

sections.title: Previous Investigations
sections.summary: Describes how data from prior subsurface investigations — including borings, field tests, groundwater records, and construction difficulty reports — can inform new site studies. Emphasizes that records from DOT, USGS, and USEPA may be publicly available and that reviewing prior work is the highest-value, lowest-cost phase of reconnaissance.
sections.body:
For studies in developed areas, subsurface conditions and selected foundation recommendations may be available from previous work for surrounding projects. Earlier site-specific data may be "dated" and while the underlying geology is unchanged, the site-specific information may have been superseded by recent activities. For example, industrialized waterfront areas near major cities may undergo cycles of expansion and reconstruction, causing subsurface conditions to change. Often old foundations and wharf structures remain buried in place. Records of former construction may contain information on borings, field tests, groundwater conditions, and potential or actual sources of construction difficulties. Note that explorations from state departments of transportation (DOT), the United States Geological Survey (USGS), and United States Environmental Protection Agency (USEPA) may be publicly available.

Review of data from previous work should receive the greatest attention of any phase in a reconnaissance investigation because it is likely very relevant. Additionally, this information generally comes at relatively little cost and allows the project team to quickly [understand site conditions].
key_points: Previous investigation data — borings, field tests, groundwater conditions — may be available for developed sites from surrounding projects.
Earlier site-specific data may be outdated if site activities (e.g., construction cycles at waterfront industrial areas) have altered subsurface conditions.
Old buried foundations and wharf structures can complicate subsurface interpretation; records of former construction are valuable.
Public agency records from DOT, USGS, and USEPA may be accessible at little or no cost.
Review of prior work should receive the greatest attention during reconnaissance because it is highly relevant and cost-effective.
sections.applicability: Applies when conducting the reconnaissance phase of a geotechnical investigation in developed areas where prior subsurface data or public agency records may exist.

sections.title: REMOTE SENSING DATA METHODS
sections.summary: Covers remote sensing methods used in geotechnical site investigation, including aerial photography, satellite imagery, radar, and thermal infrared data. Introduces both historical (pre-2019) and more recent technologies, their sources, and their application to planning boring programs, 3D terrain modeling, and augmented reality platforms.
key_points: Remote sensing encompasses aerial photography, satellite imagery, SLAR, thermal IR, and emerging digital technologies.
Historic sources (Table 2-3) generally require purchase of images; newer sources (Table 2-4) are often freely available online.
Remote sensing data can be integrated into augmented reality (AR) platforms using GIS tools and special headsets.
Aerial imagery is considered a minimal requirement for project sites with limited subsurface information.
UAVs can be used to develop digital terrain model (DTM) files and local 3D topography economically.
sections.applicability: Applies to any geotechnical project requiring preliminary site investigation using remote sensing technologies.

sections.title: Sources
sections.summary: Describes sources of remote sensing data available to geotechnical engineers, including aerial photographs (scales 1:12,000 to 1:80,000 and digital at 1:1000 or better), satellite data, and internet-based tools. Distinguishes between historical sources (Table 2-3) that typically require image purchase and newer free or internet-available technologies (Table 2-4), including their potential use in AR platforms.
sections.body:
Aerial photographs are a common type of remote sensing, including older printed images (scales from 1:12,000 to 1:80,000) and reasonably high-resolution digital images for most of the United States (scale of 1:1000 or better). Some regions possess a wealth of "historic" imagery that may extend before the current site was developed. Photos are useful for topographic and/or geologic mapping in addition to identifying drainage patterns, locations of existing structures, vegetation, access routes and site locations for planned explorations. Remote sensing also refers to non-photographic data gathering satellites, from which data, such as vegetation development, water sources, etc., are available. Table 2-3 summarizes sources and types of remote sensing data that have been historically (i.e., pre-2019) used by geotechnical engineers. The technologies identified in Table 2-3 generally require the purchase of images from the entities that generated the images.

Table 2-4 provides a summary of more recent remote sensing technologies. Data from some of these are free to the user and are often available on the internet. Data from remote sensing technology can be incorporated into developing augmented reality (AR) platforms, which provide an interactive experience where objects are projected into a perceived real-world environment. This requires computer-generated information presented in a geospatial environment through the use of special lenses and headsets.
key_points: Aerial photographs range from 1:12,000 to 1:80,000 (older printed) and 1:1000 or better (digital); historic imagery may predate current site development.
Photos support topographic/geologic mapping, drainage pattern identification, structure locations, vegetation, and access route planning.
Table 2-3 covers pre-2019 historic remote sensing sources, which typically require image purchase.
Table 2-4 covers newer technologies, many of which are freely available online.
Remote sensing data can feed augmented reality (AR) platforms via GIS tools, special lenses, and headsets.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting and obtaining remote sensing data sources for geotechnical site investigation.

sections.title: Utilization
sections.summary: Describes how remote sensing data is utilized by geotechnical engineers, emphasizing that internet-based mapping and GIS cross-section profiling tools now exceed earlier capabilities. Highlights that aerial imagery is a minimal project requirement for sites with limited information, that 3D visualization aids large engineering studies, and that UAVs can economically produce digital terrain models (DTMs) for local topography.
sections.body:
Remote sensing represents a well-adopted resource by geotechnical engineers. The emergence of internet-based mapping tools coupled with the cross-section profiling capabilities using geographic information system (GIS) tools currently exceed the capabilities and functionality of earlier tools.

For project sites where limited information is available, aerial images greatly aid in planning and layout of an appropriate boring program and currently be considered a minimal requirement for projects. For large engineering studies, including highway and airfield work, a three-dimensional (3D) visualization may be beneficial. Individual users can develop digital terrain model (DTM) files using data from UAVs data, and commercial companies can economically develop local 3D topography with the use of UAVs.
key_points: Internet-based mapping and GIS cross-section profiling tools now exceed the capabilities of earlier remote sensing tools.
Aerial imagery is considered a minimal requirement for project sites where limited subsurface information exists.
Aerial images aid in planning and layout of boring programs.
3D visualization is beneficial for large engineering studies such as highway and airfield projects.
UAVs enable individual users and commercial companies to economically develop DTM files and local 3D topography.
sections.applicability: Applies when planning a geotechnical exploration program and deciding how to leverage remote sensing data for site characterization.

sections.title: Geophysical Methods
sections.summary: Introduces geophysical investigations as an increasingly accepted approach for estimating subsurface conditions. Covers the overall scope of geophysical methods, noting improved interpretation techniques and professional acceptance. References Table 2-5 (common geophysical testing techniques and objectives) and ASTM D6429 for selection guidance. Identifies large/linear sites (dams, tunnels, highways) as best suited for these methods.
key_points: Geophysical investigations are increasingly used due to improved interpretation techniques and broader professional acceptance.
Table 2-5 summarizes common surface geophysical testing techniques and their investigation objectives.
ASTM D6429 provides guidance on selecting appropriate surface geophysical testing techniques.
Methods are best suited for large and/or linear sites such as dams, reservoirs, tunnels, highways, and large groups of structures.
Techniques are available for both onshore and offshore exploration.
Geophysics can locate gravel deposits and other construction materials, especially where stratified materials differ substantially from adjacent soil/rock.
sections.applicability: Applies when planning subsurface investigations for large, linear, or geologically complex sites where broad-area characterization is needed.

sections.title: Utilization and Applications
sections.summary: Describes the practical applications of geophysical methods in subsurface investigation. Emphasizes suitability for large/linear sites (dams, reservoirs, tunnels, highways) and their use in locating gravel deposits and stratified construction materials. References Table 2-5 for a summary of testing methods and their objectives, and ASTM D6429 for technique selection guidance. Both onshore and offshore techniques are noted.
sections.body:
With increasing regularity, geophysical investigations are being used to estimate subsurface conditions because of improved interpretation techniques and the overall acceptance within the professional community of the geophysical characterization techniques. Table 2-5 provides a summary of the common geophysical testing techniques and the objectives/characterizations that are obtained from these techniques. Information regarding the selection of appropriate surface geophysical testing techniques is also presented in ASTM D6429.

Geophysical methods are best suited when investigating relatively large and/or linear sites, including dams, reservoirs, tunnels, highways, and large groups of structures. Techniques are available for both onshore and offshore exploration. Geophysics have been used to locate gravel deposits and sources of other construction materials, particularly for stratified materials where properties differ substantially from adjacent soil/rock. As shown in Table 2-5, many of the geophysical testing methods are helpful in identifying different subsurface strata and anomalies in the subsurface.
key_points: Geophysical investigations are increasingly adopted due to improved interpretation and professional acceptance.
Table 2-5 catalogs common geophysical techniques (seismic, electrical, electromagnetic, potential field) and their investigation objectives.
ASTM D6429 governs selection of appropriate surface geophysical testing techniques.
Best suited for large and/or linear sites: dams, reservoirs, tunnels, highways, large structure groups.
Both onshore and offshore geophysical exploration techniques are available.
Particularly effective for locating stratified materials (e.g., gravel deposits) where properties differ substantially from surrounding soil/rock.
Many techniques help identify subsurface strata boundaries and anomalies.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting geophysical investigation methods for sites requiring broad subsurface characterization, especially large, linear, or offshore project areas.

sections.title: Advantages and Limitations
sections.summary: Begins a discussion of the advantages and limitations of geophysical surveys relative to conventional borings. Notes that geophysical surveys cover large areas rapidly and economically, but that results reflect average subsurface conditions over an area rather than the point-specific data obtained from a series of borings. The section continues beyond the chunk boundary.
sections.body: In contrast to borings, geophysical surveys explore large areas rapidly and economically. Because they evaluate conditions over a large area, the results reflect average conditions in an area rather than a specific result that one would obtain from a series of vertically advanced borings. Geophysical testing can prove most [continues beyond chunk].
key_points: Geophysical surveys cover large areas rapidly and economically compared to conventional borings.
Results reflect average subsurface conditions over an area, not point-specific data as obtained from individual borings.
Geophysical testing is most effective when used in conjunction with targeted borings for ground-truth verification.
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating the trade-offs between geophysical survey methods and conventional drilling/boring programs for site characterization.

sections.title: Soil and Rock Exploration Methods
sections.summary: Introduces the primary field methods for subsurface soil and rock exploration. Soil borings are identified as the most common method, enabling vertical profiling and sample collection. Rock drilling and coring are noted as more specialized. The section frames the overall coverage of drilling/boring, test pits, and other exploratory techniques addressed in the subsections.
sections.body: Soil borings are the most commonly used method for subsurface soil exploration in the field. They allow a vertical profile of soil to be established at a specific location and for the collection of samples at selected vertical intervals at specific locations. Rock drilling and coring techniques are more specialized than those used for soils and are used less frequently.
key_points: Soil borings are the most common field method for subsurface exploration, enabling vertical profiling and targeted sampling.
Rock drilling and coring are more specialized and less frequently used than soil boring methods.
This section introduces drilling/boring methods, test pits/trenches, and other downhole exploratory techniques.
sections.applicability: Applies when planning any subsurface soil or rock exploration program for geotechnical investigation.

sections.title: Drilling and Boring Methods
sections.summary: Covers the principal methods for advancing soil and rock borings, including hollow-stem augers, rotary wash, direct-push, and sonic techniques. References Tables 2-6, 2-7, and 2-8 for method applicability and equipment selection criteria based on ground conditions and drilling type. Includes Figure 2-1 schematic of various drilling techniques.
sections.body:
Most geotechnical borings in soils have historically utilized either hollow-stem augers or rotary wash techniques, where numerous variations technologies are available. Recent advancements that are gaining popularity and acceptance include the use of direct-push and sonic boring techniques. Table 2-6 identifies the applicability of the several methods for advancing soil borings. Table 2-7 provides similar information for rock.

The drilling equipment used for geotechnical investigation is selected based on a combination of: (1) ground conditions encountered at the site (i.e., soft ground, steep terrain, over water, etc.) and (2) the type of drilling that is selected (i.e., auger, rotary, percussion, etc.). Table 2-8 provides a summary of various types of drilling equipment and their application. Figure 2-1 provides a schematic of the various drilling methods.
key_points: Hollow-stem augers and rotary wash are the historically dominant methods for soil borings; direct-push and sonic techniques are gaining acceptance.
Equipment selection is driven by ground conditions (soft ground, steep terrain, over water) and drilling type (auger, rotary, percussion).
Table 2-6 summarizes soil boring method applicability; Table 2-7 covers rock drilling methods; Table 2-8 lists drilling equipment and applications.
Soil boring methods include auger boring (ASTM D1452), hollow-stem auger, wash-type, Becker hammer, bucket auger, direct push, and sonic drilling.
Rock drilling methods include rotary coring (ASTM D2113), wire-line rotary coring, swelling clay/soft rock coring, sonic drilling, and percussive methods.
Sonic drilling is applicable in nearly all soils and much bedrock, returns continuous stratigraphy, and does not require drilling fluids, but is not cost-effective in hard rock.
Becker hammer penetration test uses a 168 mm double-walled casing driven by a double-acting diesel hammer; skin friction of casing is difficult to account for.

tables: Table 2-6 – Methods of Advancing an Exploration Hole in Soil (NCHRP 2018 and Day 1999)
Table 2-7 – Rock Core Drilling Methods (NCHRP 2018 and Day 1999)
Table 2-8 – Soil and Rock Investigation Equipment and Their Applications (NCHRP 2018 and Australian Drilling Industry Training Committee 2015)
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting drilling or boring methods and equipment for geotechnical site investigation in soil or rock.

sections.title: Boring Layout and Depth
sections.summary: Provides general guidance on the number, location, and depth of geotechnical borings by structure type, referencing Table 2-9. Covers bridges (shallow and deep foundations), retaining structures, roadway embankments and cuts, pavements, culverts, and poles/towers. Emphasizes that site geology and regional experience must inform boring layout, and that at least two borings per critical stratum are needed for settlement, slope stability, or seepage analyses.
sections.body:
General guidance for preliminary and final boring layout (i.e., location and number of borings) and the depth of the borings is presented in Table 2-9 according to the type of structure and/or problem being investigated. Additional discussion of the spacing and number of borings is presented in FHWA (2002). In addition to structure type, boring layout and depth are strongly dependent on past experience in the region (or at the site) and the site/region geology. When a project is in an unfamiliar area, at least one boring should extend well below the zone necessary for apparent stability to verify that the site conditions are consistent with the anticipated geology and to assure no unusual or unanticipated condition exist at depth.

The site geology is an important factor in developing the boring layout and should influence the arrangement of borings so that geological sections may be viewed in the context of the final design. This requires review of geologic maps of the area and compilation of the information in a format that allows the geology, existing topography, current site plans, and boring locations to be presented at similar scales on the same figure/drawing.

In cases where detailed settlement, slope stability, or seepage analyses are required, the boring plan should include a minimum of two borings in each critical stratum to obtain intact samples (if applicable). For some site investigation programs this may mean that preliminary sample borings and/or cone penetration soundings may be needed to determine the most representative location and depth for intact sample borings.
key_points: Table 2-9 provides minimum boring numbers and depths by project type (bridges, retaining walls, roadways, pavements, culverts, poles/towers).
Boring layout and depth depend on structure type, regional/site experience, and site geology; geological sections should be viewable in context of final design.
In unfamiliar areas, at least one boring should extend well below the apparent stability zone to confirm anticipated geology.
For settlement, slope stability, or seepage analyses, a minimum of two borings per critical stratum is required to obtain intact samples.
Bridge shallow foundation depths: 2B for L≤2B, 3B for 2B≤L≤5B, 4B for L≥5B (B = footing width, L = footing length); extend 10 ft into competent rock if encountered first.
Retaining structures: borings extend 2x wall height below wall bottom or 10 ft into hard rock; anchored and soil nail walls require additional anchorage zone borings.
Roadway embankments: boring depth of 2x embankment height; pavements require minimum 10 ft below proposed top of subgrade.
tables: Table 2-9 – Selecting Number, Locations, and Depths of Investigation (after NCHRP 2018, FHWA 2002, FHWA 2016, NYDOT 2013, and SCDOT 2010)
sections.applicability: Applies when determining the number, spacing, and minimum depths of soil borings for any geotechnical investigation program based on project type.

sections.title: Abandoning or Sealing Boreholes
sections.summary: Specifies requirements for backfilling and sealing boreholes after geotechnical investigation. Backfilling with drill cuttings is often sufficient, but grouting is mandatory for borings below the water table, artesian conditions, and environmental borings. Covers temporary open-hole use for water-level observations, annular space backfill requirements, and references agency-specific guidelines from USACE and state DOTs.
sections.body: Boreholes should be backfilled. Often, backfilling with the drill cuttings is sufficient. However, boreholes must be sealed with grout in cases where the borings are advanced below groundwater, in all cases where artesian pressures are encountered, and whenever environmental borings are advanced. Under these conditions, boreholes may be left temporarily unfilled to use for water-level observations after the initial field investigation drilling is completed. In boreholes for groundwater observations, the casings should be placed in tight contact with walls of boreholes or the annular space between the standpipe and borehole should be backfilled using the appropriately graded sand or gravel. Many agencies, such as the USACE and state DOTs have specific guidelines for sealing boreholes, and these are part of the project specifications. Additional discussion of details regarding groundwater investigation is presented in Section 2-8.
key_points: All boreholes must be backfilled; drill cuttings are often sufficient for dry, non-artesian conditions.
Grout sealing is mandatory when borings penetrate below the water table, encounter artesian pressures, or are environmental borings.
Boreholes may be left temporarily open for water-level observation before final sealing.
Annular space between standpipe and borehole wall must be backfilled with appropriately graded sand or gravel for groundwater observation wells.
USACE and state DOTs have specific borehole sealing guidelines that become part of project specifications; see Section 2-8 for groundwater investigation details.
sections.applicability: Applies when closing out geotechnical boreholes, particularly those advanced below the water table or under artesian conditions, or used for environmental investigation.

sections.title: Test Pits and Test Trenches
sections.summary: Describes the use of test pits and test trenches for shallow subsurface exploration and sampling. Test pits are used to assess near-surface conditions, groundwater depth, topsoil thickness, and construction material sources. Test trenches are elongated pits suited for heterogeneous deposits, fault trace detection, and landslide plane investigation. References Table 2-10 for use and limitations, and notes the importance of hand-cut block sampling for sensitive or structured soils.
sections.body:
Test pits are commonly used to examine and sample soils in situ at relatively shallow depths. Test pits can be used to determine the depth to shallow groundwater, thickness of topsoil or surficial deposits, and/or to assess near surface conditions. Test pits are often used to determine sources of construction materials for earthwork projects, such as dams and embankments. Test pits range from shallow, hand-excavated pits or (more commonly) machine-advanced excavations.

Test trenches are essentially long test pits and are particularly useful for exploration in very heterogeneous deposits (e.g., rubble fills) where borings may be misleading, meaningless, or not feasible. Test trenches are used commonly for detection of fault traces in seismicity investigations and for investigating conditions near a slide plane in a landslide investigation. Safety precautions need to be recognized when working in and around test pits and trenches.

Table 2-10 provides guidance for the use and limitations of test pits and trenches. Hand-cut, block samples are frequently obtained from these explorations and may be necessary for sensitive soils, brittle and weathered rock, and soil formations exhibiting a honeycomb structure.
key_points: Test pits assess near-surface conditions, shallow groundwater depth, topsoil thickness, and construction material sources; can be hand-excavated or machine-advanced.
Test trenches (elongated test pits) are preferred for heterogeneous deposits (e.g., rubble fills) where borings would be misleading or infeasible.
Test trenches are commonly used for fault trace detection in seismic investigations and landslide plane investigation.
Safety precautions are essential when working in and around test pits and trenches.
Hand-cut block samples from test pits/trenches are necessary for sensitive soils, brittle/weathered rock, and honeycomb-structured soils.
Table 2-10 provides guidance on the use and limitations of test pits and trenches.
tables: Table 2-10 – Guidance for the use and limitations of test pits and trenches
sections.applicability: Applies when shallow subsurface exploration is needed, particularly for heterogeneous deposits, fault investigations, landslide studies, or construction material source identification.

sections.title: Other Exploratory Techniques
sections.summary: Describes downhole tools and instruments that can be deployed in an open borehole after drilling. Covers borehole cameras for rock stratigraphy and strike/dip assessment, and geotechnical performance monitoring instruments including slope inclinometers, water pressure transducers, and borehole extensometers.
sections.body: Once a hole is advanced in either soil or rock, downhole tools can be placed in the open hole to make specific measurements or serve as carriers for geophysical testing instruments. Borehole cameras are commonly used for open holes in rock to assess stratigraphy, as well as strike and dip of the formation. Geotechnical performance monitoring instruments (i.e., slope inclinometers, water pressure transducers, borehole extensometers, etc.) can also be placed in the advanced borehole.
key_points: Downhole tools deployed in open boreholes can make specific measurements or carry geophysical testing instruments.
Borehole cameras assess rock stratigraphy and determine strike and dip of formations.
Geotechnical monitoring instruments—slope inclinometers, water pressure transducers, and borehole extensometers—can be installed in completed boreholes.
sections.applicability: Applies after a borehole has been advanced in soil or rock when additional in-hole measurements or geotechnical monitoring instrument installation is required.

sections.title: Sampling
sections.summary: Introduces soil and rock sampling concepts, distinguishing between disturbed and intact (undisturbed) samples. Explains that disturbance is inherent to the sampling process, that disturbed samples serve index/classification testing while intact samples are needed for strength, compressibility, and permeability tests. Notes that sample number and type depend on stratification, material type, quantity needed, and project criticality.
sections.body:
Recovery of representative samples of the subsurface soil and rock for testing is perhaps the most common goal of the techniques in Section 2-5. These samples are commonly referenced as disturbed or undisturbed depending on how well the recovered sample maintains the structure of the in situ material. Disturbance is initiated by the process of removing the soil/rock from the confined conditions in the subsurface. Thus, an "undisturbed" sample is actually a misnomer, as it (hopefully) represents a minimally (or nominally) disturbed sample. The term intact sample has largely replaced undisturbed sample in geotechnical engineering vernacular.

Disturbed samples are primarily used for index tests that are performed for classification. A disturbed sample needs only to be representative of the soil composition and moisture because the soil structure is disturbed. Intact samples are obtained primarily for laboratory strength, compressibility, and permeability tests. The in situ structure and composition significantly influence the strength, compressibility and permeability (i.e., engineering) properties of the soil. Most of the discussion in this section focuses on sampling from terrestrial or shallow-water locations. Offshore samplers are specialized and are treated separately in Section 2-6.3.

The number and type of samples depend on the stratification of the subsurface, the type of material encountered, the quantity needed for testing, and the criticality of the application. For most projects, both disturbed and intact samples are obtained for testing.
key_points: "Undisturbed" is a misnomer; the preferred term is 'intact sample,' reflecting that some disturbance is unavoidable.
Disturbed samples are used for index/classification tests; intact samples are required for strength, compressibility, and permeability testing.
The in situ structure and composition significantly influence engineering properties of soil.
Sample number and type depend on stratification, material type, quantity needed, and project criticality.
Offshore sampling is specialized and covered separately in Section 2-6.3.
sections.applicability: Applies to any geotechnical investigation requiring representative subsurface soil or rock samples for classification or engineering property testing.

sections.title: Soil Sampling
sections.summary: Parent section covering soil sampling methods, divided into disturbed and intact soil sampling subsections. Addresses the range of sampler types and conditions applicable to fine-grained soils, sands, gravels, and other soil types encountered during subsurface investigation.
key_points: Soil sampling is categorized into disturbed and intact methods, each suited to different testing objectives.
Sampler selection depends on soil type, consistency, and the level of disturbance that can be tolerated.
sections.applicability: Applies whenever soil samples must be collected from boreholes or excavations for geotechnical testing.

sections.title: Disturbed Soil Samples
sections.summary: Covers methods and samplers for obtaining representative disturbed soil samples. Specifies that samples are collected at minimum 5-ft vertical intervals and at every stratum change. Details the split barrel (split spoon) sampler as the most common device, and lists other sampler types (continuous helical-flight auger, bucket auger, Large Penetration Test) with their dimensions, best-use soils, and limitations.
sections.body: In general, representative disturbed samples are obtained at vertical intervals of no less than 5 feet and at every change in strata. Continuous samples are occasionally required or justified. This may be the case when a relatively thin layer of critical material is anticipated. Table 2-11 lists common types of disturbed samples and samplers. Recommended procedures for obtaining disturbed samples are provided in ASTM D1586. The split barrel (a.k.a., split spoon) sampler, depicted in Figure 2-2, is the most commonly used sampler.
key_points: Disturbed samples collected at ≥5-ft intervals and at every stratum change; continuous sampling justified for thin critical layers.
The split barrel (split spoon) sampler is the most common disturbed sampler; used in the Standard Penetration Test (SPT) per ASTM D1586.
Gravel-sized particles and larger are the primary cause of low recovery for split barrel samplers.
Continuous helical-flight and bucket augers are rotation-based; effective above the water table in most soils.
The Large Penetration Test (LPT) uses 2–3-inch ID samplers driven by up to 300-lb hammer; results are not equivalent to SPT N-values due to non-standardized equipment.
sections.applicability: Applies when collecting disturbed soil samples for index testing and soil classification during borehole investigations.

sections.title: Intact Soil Samples
sections.summary: Describes methods and criteria for obtaining intact (undisturbed) soil samples, primarily using the thin-walled Shelby tube per ASTM D1587. Defines acceptance criteria: no visible distortion, >95% recovery ratio, <15% area ratio, and <3% clearance ratio. Covers specialized samplers (fixed piston, foil, hydraulic piston, Denison, Pitcher) for soft to stiff fine-grained soils, and explains why intact sampling of clean sands and gravels is generally not feasible.
sections.body:
Intact (or "undisturbed") samples are most commonly obtained using a thin-walled steel tube (Shelby tube) that is pushed at a relatively rapid and constant rate following procedures in accordance with ASTM D1587. Intact sampling and samplers should provide samples that comply with the following criteria: (1) show no visible distortion of strata, (2) include no visible openings or softened material, (3) exhibit a recovery ratio (i.e., sample length divided by distance of sample push) that exceeds 95 percent, (4) have an area ratio (i.e., area displaced by the sampler tube divided by the area of the sample) of less than 15 percent, and (5) have a clearance ratio (i.e., the difference between the diameter of inside of the tube and the diameter of the opening at the bottom of the tube divided by the diameter of the opening at the bottom of the tube) as small as possible but less than 3 percent. A schematic and photograph of a thin-walled Shelby tube that meets these criteria is presented in Figure 2-3.

In general, intact samples of clean sands and gravels cannot be obtained, even when using thin-walled samplers. For this reason, in situ testing methods are commonly used in these soils, and intact sampling focuses on silts, clays, and coarse-grained soils with a significant amount of silty and clayey fines. Because fine-grained soils can vary from very soft to very hard, different types of samplers have been developed to facilitate the recovery of intact samples. Table 2-12 summarizes common types of samplers used for intact soil samples.

For soft soils, a stationary (or fixed-piston) sampler or hydraulic piston sampler is commonly deployed. For very soft soils and varved clays, a foil sampler may be deployed, although limited in use in the United States.

For stiff fine-grained soils, or for layers of soft and hard materials, special samplers have been developed that have the ability to "core" around the recovered stiff materials while capturing the softer materials in the same thin-walled tube. The Denison sampler and the Pitcher sampler are two types of common samplers for these subsurface conditions.
key_points: Primary intact sampler is the thin-walled Shelby tube (ASTM D1587), pushed at a rapid, constant rate.
Acceptance criteria: no visible strata distortion, recovery ratio >95%, area ratio <15%, clearance ratio <3%.
Intact samples of clean sands and gravels are generally not obtainable; in situ testing is preferred for these soils.
Fixed/stationary piston and hydraulic piston (Osterberg) samplers are used for soft to medium clays and fine silts.
Foil sampler is used for very soft sensitive clays, silts, and varved clays; limited use in the US.
Denison and Pitcher samplers are designed for stiff fine-grained soils and interlayered soft/hard materials.
sections.applicability: Applies when collecting intact soil samples for laboratory strength, compressibility, or permeability testing, particularly in fine-grained soils.

sections.title: Intact Samples from Test Pits and Test Trenches
sections.summary: Describes the procedure for obtaining hand-trimmed block samples from the floors or sidewalls of test pits and trenches. Block samples are considered the least disturbed sample type achievable. The method involves trimming a soil column to fit a transport container, minimizing annular space, and sealing with wax. Applicable only to shallow depths accessible by test pits.
sections.body:
One of the advantages of test pits and test trenches is that hand-trimmed (i.e., block) samples may be obtained from the bottom or the sidewalls of the test pits and test trenches. These block samples are potentially the least disturbed of all types of samples. Unfortunately, the test pits and trenches are only feasible to a limited depth.

To obtain a block sample, a column of soil is trimmed the same size or slightly smaller than the container that will be used for transporting the sample. The container should be placed over the top of the sample and should provide as small an annular space as possible. This annular space ideally would be filled using wax. A tight fit in a stiff container that can be sealed provides the ideal conditions for retrieving and transporting block samples with least disturbance.
key_points: Block samples from test pits and trenches are the least disturbed sample type available in geotechnical practice.
Samples are hand-trimmed to match or be slightly smaller than the transport container.
Annular space between sample and container should be minimized and ideally filled with wax.
Technique is limited to shallow depths accessible by test pits or trenches.
sections.applicability: Applies when obtaining the highest-quality (least disturbed) soil samples from shallow test pits or trenches for critical laboratory testing.

sections.title: Rock Sampling
sections.summary: Covers rock core sampling using tungsten carbide or diamond core bits, standard casing and core barrel sizes, and the use of single, double, and triple tube core barrels. Discusses Rock Quality Designation (RQD) and percentage core recovery as indicators of rock soundness and weathering. Addresses challenges of sampling highly weathered, fractured, or disintegrated rock near the soil-rock interface.
sections.body:
Rock is sampled with core barrels that have either tungsten carbide or diamond core bits at the cutting face. Drill rods and core barrels come in a variety of standard sizes (see Table 2-13), depending on the size of the recovered rock core.

For hard and massive rock, relatively undisturbed rock samples may be obtained using just the core barrel to recover the sample. More commonly, a tube (or series of tubes) is used to contain the rock core and the tube is isolated from the core barrel to minimize disturbance. Inner tubes must be used for undisturbed rock sampling whenever the rock includes discontinuities. Table 2-14 lists summarizes techniques for recovery of relatively undisturbed samples of rock.

Double tube core barrels are the most commonly used in practice. Depending on the number of discontinuities in the rock, the recovered sample may be considered either disturbed or undisturbed. Schematics of single and double tube rock core samplers are provided in Figure 2-5(a) and (b), respectively.

The suitability of rock cores for structural property tests depends on the quality of individual recovered samples. If the properties of the intact rock are desired, then smaller diameter cores are recommended because large-diameter rock cores likely include more discontinuities than small-diameter rock cores.

The percentage of core recovery (i.e., recovered core length divided by the recorded core run) provides an indication of soundness and degree of weathering of rock. The Rock Quality Designation, RQD, (i.e., total length of recovered core pieces greater than 4 inches in length divided by the recorded core run) provide a better indication of the soundness and degree of rock weathering because it essentially disallows the consideration of the fractured and weathered rock intervals. The RQD is also a major factor in assessing the behavior of the in situ rock mass, as defined by the Rock Mass Rating (RMR) of the rock. The engineer and geologist should carefully examine rock core samples exhibiting low recovery and/or low RQD to assess the reasons for low recovery and the interpreted poor rock quality. Details regarding on rock classification and rock properties are presented in Chapter 1 and in NCHRP (2018).

Sampling of highly (or partially) weathered, fractured, or disintegrated rock is extremely difficult. These materials often occur near the interface between soil and rock and represent the transition between these two materials, especially in the case of residual soils. The best samples of these materials are obtained by experienced drillers using double- or triple-core barrel samplers.
key_points: Rock is cored using tungsten carbide or diamond bits; standard sizes are EX, AX, BX, and NX (per ASTM D2113).
Inner tubes must be used for undisturbed rock sampling when the rock contains discontinuities; double tube barrels are most common.
Triple tube core barrels with split inner liners best preserve intensely fractured rock core.
Percentage core recovery = recovered core length / core run; indicates overall rock soundness.
RQD = total length of core pieces >4 inches / core run; better indicator of soundness, disregarding fractured/weathered intervals.
RQD is a primary input to Rock Mass Rating (RMR) for assessing in situ rock mass behavior.
Smaller diameter cores are preferred when intact rock properties are needed, as larger cores are more likely to include discontinuities.
Highly weathered, fractured, or disintegrated rock near the soil-rock interface requires experienced drillers with double- or triple-tube samplers.
sections.applicability: Applies to geotechnical investigations requiring rock core samples for classification, quality assessment, or structural property testing.

sections.title: Offshore Sampling
sections.summary: Addresses sampling of soil and rock from underwater environments including rivers, lakes, and the ocean. For depths less than ~60 ft, conventional equipment on jack-up platforms or barges is used. Deeper or extreme ocean settings require dedicated drill ships and specialized equipment. Covers oceanographic sampler types (open-tube, piston, vibratory, gravity corers) and notes limitations including large length-to-diameter ratios and gas exsolution upon sample recovery.
sections.body:
In some cases, samples of soil and rock must be obtained from the bottom of rivers, lakes, or the ocean. For water depths less than about 60 feet, the conventional soil and rock boring equipment can be used on small jack-up platforms, small barges, or barrel floats. The challenge is that floating equipment requires suitable anchoring and is limited to fairly calm water, although tidal fluctuations can be easily accommodated. For deep water sites and/or extreme ocean settings, large dedicated drill ships, specialized equipment, and experience are required to obtain quality intact samples. Table 2-15 identifies some of the specialized equipment used for underwater sampling.

Numerous types of oceanographic samplers, both open-tube and piston types, are available for use when drilling from ships. Some of these depend upon free-fall penetration and are limited in the depth of exploration. Drilling and sampling from the ocean floor can be accomplished using specialized equipment deployed remotely from portable equipment that is deployed in underwater vessels or on underwater platforms operating on the ocean floor. The quality of samples obtained by most oceanographic samplers is not high because of their large length to diameter ratio and because air/gas in the dissolved state in the underwater environment comes out of solution when the sample is recovered at the ground surface. For detailed information on underwater sampling equipment, refer to ASTM STP 501 (ASTM 1972).
key_points: For water depths <~60 ft, conventional boring equipment on jack-up platforms, barges, or barrel floats can be used.
Deep water or extreme ocean settings require dedicated drill ships and specialized experience.
Floating equipment is limited to calm water and requires suitable anchoring, though tidal fluctuations are manageable.
Oceanographic sampler types include open-tube gravity corers, piston gravity corers, vibratory corers, Peterson dredge grabs, and Pflueger corers.
Sample quality from most oceanographic samplers is low due to large L/D ratios and gas exsolution upon retrieval.
Detailed reference for underwater sampling: ASTM STP 501 (ASTM 1972).
sections.applicability: Applies to geotechnical investigations requiring subsurface sampling from beneath rivers, lakes, or ocean environments.

sections.title: Field Logging and Boring Logs
sections.summary: Describes the preparation of field and final engineering boring logs during and after drilling and sampling operations. The field log records boring ID, date, personnel, advancement method, sample depths and types, SPT N-values, water level observations, GPS coordinates, and preliminary stratigraphy. The final boring log is the official engineering record, with soils classified per USCS (ASTM D2487/D2488), AASHTO, or USDA systems.
sections.body:
While monitoring drilling and sampling activities, an engineer, geologist, or experienced driller prepares a field boring log to document the findings and observations. This field logging is an important part of documenting the soil and rock conditions that exist at the project site. A typical field log includes all the relevant information for the boring that was completed, including a unique boring identification number, date of drilling, personnel on-site, boring advancement method (i.e., auger, rotary wash, direct push, sonic), depths where samples were obtained, type of samples (i.e., split-barrel and Shelby tube), hammer type, raw SPT N values, water level observations, and preliminary estimates of stratigraphy. If available, the global positioning system (GPS) coordinates should be included. The field log provides a unique designation of each recovered sample, whether disturbed or intact, as well as a field visual classification of the sample in accordance with ASTM D2488.

The field log, the recovered samples, and lab/field testing results are used to produce the final boring log, which represents the official engineering record of the drilling and sampling efforts. The boring log provides the permanent, technical documentation of the materials encountered during drilling, sampling, and coring. The geotechnical engineer or geologist uses the results from the field and their training/experience to group samples/records together based on color, soil type, and SPT N values and identify layers or strata, which may be consistently found in the adjacent companion borings from the site. An example of the engineering boring log is shown as Figure 2-6. In the final engineering boring logs, soil types are categorized according to a user- or agency-specified soil classification system. The most common soil classification systems in the United States include the Unified Soil Classification System (USCS) (ASTM D2487 or D2488), the AASHTO system, and the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) system.
key_points: A field boring log is prepared in real time by an engineer, geologist, or experienced driller to document drilling and sampling activities.
Field log contents include boring ID, date, personnel, advancement method, sample depths/types, hammer type, raw SPT N-values, water level, and GPS coordinates.
Field visual classification of samples follows ASTM D2488.
The final engineering boring log is the official permanent record, incorporating lab/field test results and finalized stratigraphy.
Soil classification in final logs follows USCS (ASTM D2487/D2488), AASHTO, or USDA systems, as specified by the user or agency.
sections.applicability: Applies to all geotechnical drilling and sampling programs requiring documentation of subsurface conditions through field and final boring logs.

sections.title: Penetration Resistance Tests
sections.summary: Introduces the four main in situ penetration resistance tests covered in this section: the Standard Penetration Test (SPT), Cone Penetration Test (CPT), Flat Plate Dilatometer (DMT), and Dynamic Cone Penetrometer (DCP). Each test is briefly characterized by its mechanism and common applications in subsurface characterization.
sections.body: Penetration resistance tests are the most common in situ testing techniques for characterizing subsurface conditions. The most common field penetration test remains the Standard Penetration Test (SPT), which measures resistance to the penetration of a standard, thick-walled drive sampler in an open borehole using a drop hammer. A more controlled and increasingly popular test is the Cone Penetration Test (CPT), which utilizes a standard cone-shaped instrument that is pushed at a standard constant rate from the ground surface. Another common test is the flat plate dilatometer (DMT). This device utilizes a robust steel blade that is pushed into the ground at a constant rate and then periodically stopped to allow the controlled measured inflation of a flexible steel membrane. In many parts of the United States, particularly when stiff soils and/or granular soils are encountered, a dynamic cone penetration (DCP) test is performed by driving a standard sized cone into the ground using a drop hammer. This section provides information regarding these four penetration tests. Section 2-9 will address other common in situ testing methods.
key_points: Four primary penetration resistance tests are covered: SPT, CPT, DMT, and DCP.
SPT uses a drop hammer to drive a split-barrel sampler in an open borehole.
CPT pushes an instrumented cone at a constant rate for a continuous resistance record.
DMT uses a pushed flat blade with a measured membrane inflation at intervals.
DCP drives a standard cone with a drop hammer, often in near-surface or granular soils.
Additional in situ testing methods are addressed in Section 2-9.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting or comparing in situ penetration resistance test methods for subsurface characterization.

sections.title: Standard Penetration Test (SPT)
sections.summary: Describes the SPT procedure, which drives a split-barrel sampler 18 inches into the ground using a drop hammer, recording the blow count (N value) over the last 12 inches. References ASTM D1586 and Figure 2-7. Notes the test's widespread use in the US due to large historical datasets and published correlations in Chapter 8, despite known limitations.
sections.body:
The SPT was originally developed in the 1900s and proceeds by driving a thick-walled, split-barrel (a.k.a., 'split spoon') sampler into the ground using incremental blows from a drop hammer. The sampler is driven a total of 18 inches into the ground. The number of blows required to drive the sampler the 12-inch vertical interval between 6 and 18 inches is referred to as an N value or the blow count. The procedure is presented in ASTM D1586, and a schematic of the SPT is presented in Figure 2-7.

The SPT provides a disturbed sample of the tested material and generates useful data that can be used to correlate to many engineering properties. Many factors can affect the SPT results, and there are several vastly superior in situ testing methods. Nevertheless, the test is still almost universally referenced and often required in the United States. One reason for this is the large amount of historical (i.e., legacy) data available. Numerous correlations have been published (see Chapter 8) and their use along with SPT represents the Standard of Practice in many parts of the country.
key_points: SPT drives a split-barrel sampler 18 inches total; N value is blows over the final 12 inches (6 to 18 inches).
Procedure standardized in ASTM D1586.
Provides a disturbed sample and data correlatable to many engineering properties.
Near-universal acceptance in the US driven by large legacy datasets and published correlations.
Multiple superior in situ testing methods exist, but SPT remains Standard of Practice in many regions.
sections.applicability: Applies when using or interpreting the Standard Penetration Test for subsurface investigation in standard US engineering practice.

sections.title: Corrections to Field Blow Counts
sections.summary: Explains corrections applied to raw SPT N values to account for hammer energy efficiency. Modern automatic hammers deliver consistent energy and are measured periodically. Field N values are corrected to N60 (60% efficiency baseline) and may be further normalized for overburden stress to yield (N1)60, which is used extensively in correlations presented in Chapter 8.
sections.body: As an improvement on older donut and safety hammers, most current SPT programs use an automatic hammer that does not rely on an operator-dependent cathead and rope to establish the drop height of the hammer. Modern automatic hammers deliver consistent energy to the sampler, which should be measured periodically. The field-recorded N values may be adjusted to reflect the energy of the specific hammer. The adjustments are intended to correct the N value to the 60 percent hammer efficiency that is assumed for the older equipment and historic correlations. The energy corrected value (N60) can also be normalized to an equivalent value at a vertical stress of one atmosphere. The 'overburden corrected' or 'normalized' blow count is labeled (N1)60 or N1,60. Several correlations to normalized blow count are presented in Chapter 8 and in McGregor and Duncan (1998).
key_points: Modern automatic hammers replaced older donut/safety hammer systems and deliver more consistent energy.
Field N values are corrected to N60, representing 60% hammer efficiency assumed for historic correlations.
N60 can be further normalized for overburden stress (one atmosphere) to yield (N1)60.
Normalized blow count (N1)60 is used in numerous engineering correlations in Chapter 8.
Hammer energy should be measured periodically to ensure correction accuracy.
sections.applicability: Applies when correcting raw SPT blow counts for hammer energy efficiency and overburden stress normalization.

sections.title: Advantages and Limitations
sections.summary: Summarizes the key advantages and limitations of the SPT. The primary advantage is near-universal acceptance and a large correlation dataset. Limitations include sensitivity to operational factors, gravel presence, cementation, and inability to reflect fractures or slickensides in clays. Table 2-16 catalogs operational factors known to influence field N values.
sections.body:
The biggest advantage to the SPT is its near-universal acceptance and use in the United States. As a result, there is a large data set that can be used for correlation.

However, SPT blow counts are affected by many operational procedures, the presence of gravel, and by cementation between the particle grains. In clays, the blow count does not reflect the influence of fractures or slickensides. Table 2-16 presents a summary of the many operational factors that are known to influence the N value measured in the field.
key_points: Primary advantage: near-universal US acceptance and large legacy correlation dataset.
SPT N values are sensitive to numerous operational factors, gravel presence, and cementation.
In clays, SPT cannot capture effects of fractures or slickensides.
Table 2-16 catalogues causes, effects, and directional influence (increase/decrease) on N value for common operational issues.
Driving sampler above casing bottom or in disturbed soil greatly increases N values.
Failure to maintain adequate head of water in borehole can cause the borehole bottom to go quick, decreasing N values.
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating the reliability of SPT results and identifying potential sources of error in field blow count measurements.

sections.title: Cone Penetrometer Tests (CPT)
sections.summary: Introduces the CPT family of tests, which hydraulically push an instrumented steel probe at a constant rate to obtain continuous records of cone tip resistance and sleeve friction without producing a borehole or samples. Covers the evolution from the mechanical 'Dutch' cone to modern electronic CPT, CPTu (with piezometer), and SCPTu (seismic) variants, standardized in ASTM D5778.
sections.body:
The CPT involves hydraulically pushing an instrumented steel probe at a constant rate to obtain a continuous record of the penetration resistance of the cone tip and the frictional resistance of the soil. The CPT does not produce a borehole, samples, or drill cuttings. The original test involved a mechanically operated cone, referenced as a 'Dutch' cone (DPT). The original equipment has been superseded, modified, and improved to allow electronic measurements.

Most modern instruments also include a piezometer near the tip. When equipped with the proper sensors and instruments, the routine performance of the CPT also allows the measurement of temperature, vertical alignment, electrical resistivity, acoustic emissions, and shear wave velocity.

Testing is currently conducted in accordance with ASTM D5778. The test can be conducted without the use of a pore pressure measurement and is referenced simply as the CPT. Alternatively (and commonly) the test is performed using a device to measure pore pressures behind the tip of the probe while pushing. This is referred to as the piezocone test (CPTu). Recent advances have allowed the ability to measure the propagation of shear waves using a seismic piezocone, which is referred to as a seismic CPT (SCPTu).
key_points: CPT hydraulically pushes an instrumented probe at constant rate; no borehole, samples, or drill cuttings produced.
Evolved from mechanical 'Dutch' cone to modern electronic CPT, CPTu (pore pressure), and SCPTu (seismic) variants.
Standardized in ASTM D5778.
CPTu measures pore pressures behind the tip (u2 position) during penetration.
SCPTu adds shear wave velocity measurement capability.
Modern cones can also measure temperature, resistivity, acoustic emissions, and vertical alignment.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting or specifying CPT-family tests for continuous subsurface profiling without borehole sampling.

sections.title: Equipment and Testing Procedure
sections.summary: Details the equipment components and testing procedures for CPT, including the standard 10-cm2 cone geometry (1.4-inch diameter, 60° apex), dedicated CPT trucks (20–25 tons), hydraulic advancement at 2 cm/s, water pressure transducer for CPTu, and geophone placement for SCPTu shear wave velocity measurement. References Figure 2-8 for example test record.
sections.body:
The cone penetration test requires continuous hydraulic advancement of the probe and the simultaneous recording of multiple electronic instruments. Specific equipment and procedures necessary for performing a CPT are summarized as follows:

• Cone Penetrometer: A standard cone penetrometer is a 1.4-inch (35.7-mm) diameter cylindrical probe with a 60° apex at the tip, which results in a projected tip area of 1.55 in2 (10 cm2) and a 23.3 in2 (150 cm2) instrumented sleeve surface area. Other sizes (both smaller and larger) are available. The size of a cone is typically identified by the projected tip area (i.e., 10-cm2 cone or a 15-cm2 cone). A variety of tip load capacities (i.e., 2-ton, 15-ton, etc.) are available.

• Drill Rig/CPT Truck and Cone Rods: A hydraulic actuator is attached to a truck or drill rig that can provide sufficient reaction mass to advance the penetrometer at a constant rate of 2 cm/second. This reaction can be provided using a conventional drilling rig, but dedicated CPT trucks typically weighing 20 to 25 tons have become the standard.

• Water Pressure Transducer: Valuable information can be provided by measuring the pore water pressure behind the cone tip during penetration. For a CPTu, the water pressures are monitored using a transducer and porous filter element.

• Geophone: For the SCPTu, a geophone is located along the drill string at a distance of approximately 20 inches (500 mm) above the cone tip. The geophone detects shear waves generated at the ground surface at specific vertical intervals. During advancement of the seismic cone, a shear wave is generated at the ground surface. An average shear wave velocity of the soils between the ground surface and the geophone can be calculated.

An example record from a CPT sounding is shown in Figure 2-8. This shows a schematic of the CPT probe and the near-continuous vertical profile of cone tip resistance (qt), sleeve friction (fs), and pore pressure at the u2 position (behind the tip).
key_points: Standard cone: 1.4-inch (35.7-mm) diameter, 60° apex, 10 cm2 projected tip area, 150 cm2 sleeve area.
Penetrometer advanced at constant 2 cm/second using hydraulic actuator on CPT truck or drill rig.
Dedicated CPT trucks (20–25 tons) provide required reaction mass and are the current standard.
CPTu water pressure transducer measures pore pressure at the u2 position (behind the tip).
SCPTu geophone is placed ~20 inches (500 mm) above the cone tip to detect surface-generated shear waves.
Continuous vertical profile of qt, fs, and u2 pore pressure is recorded (see Figure 2-8).
sections.applicability: Applies when specifying or reviewing CPT/CPTu/SCPTu equipment setup and field testing procedures.

sections.title: Soil Classification with CPT
sections.summary: Describes how CPT data can be used for soil classification through Soil Behavior Type (SBT) correlations. References Figure 2-9 (Robertson 2009 nine-zone normalized SBT chart) as a common method to relate CPT results to soil type. Notes that the near-continuous stratigraphic profile enables estimation of strength, compressibility, modulus, and hydraulic conductivity, with correlations in Chapter 8.
sections.body:
Regardless of the specific type of cone penetration test probe (i.e., CPT, CPTu, SCPTu), the testing concept has gained near universal acceptance and interest. As shown in Figure 2-8, a near-continuous vertical profile of the stratigraphic variations is obtained. A variety of engineering parameters can be estimated from CPT results. Many correlations of CPT data to strength, compressibility, modulus, hydraulic conductivity, and other properties are available, some of which are provided in Chapter 8.

The CPT is able to estimate the soil type of the deposit penetrated. A common method for doing this is shown in Figure 2-9, which relates soil behavior type (SBT) to specific CPT results. This type of correlation is extremely useful for site characterization and subsurface stratigraphy. Other soil type correlations are available.
key_points: CPT provides a near-continuous vertical stratigraphic profile useful for site characterization.
Soil Behavior Type (SBT) classification can be estimated from CPT results using the Robertson 2009 nine-zone normalized chart (Figure 2-9).
CPT correlations to strength, compressibility, modulus, and hydraulic conductivity are provided in Chapter 8.
SBT correlations are applicable to all CPT probe variants (CPT, CPTu, SCPTu).
sections.applicability: Applies when using CPT data to classify soil type and estimate engineering parameters for site characterization.

sections.title: Advantages and Limitations
sections.summary: Summarizes the advantages and limitations of CPT-family tests. Advantages include speed, continuous soil condition record, and a wide range of published correlations. Limitations include no sample recovery, difficulty advancing in dense or hard soils with risk of probe damage, and reliance on specialty vendors for electronic instrumentation.
sections.body:
The CPT provides numerous advantages, due to its popularity in engineering practice and proliferation of useful correlations to other engineering parameters. The test can be performed quickly. The speed of operation allows considerable data to be obtained in a short period of time, resulting in a continuous record of soil conditions. It is particularly helpful in assessing variability in subsurface conditions across a site.

The major limitation of all cone penetration tests is that discrete samples are not recovered for physical observation and companion testing. The cone can be difficult to advance in dense or stiff to hard soils, and if the operator is not experienced, the probe can be damaged (or destroyed) when encountering these materials. The specialized equipment and the reliance on electronic instrumentation usually requires the services of a specialty vendor to perform the tests.
key_points: CPT is fast, providing continuous soil condition records and enabling rapid site variability assessment.
Proliferation of published correlations makes CPT widely useful for engineering parameter estimation.
No discrete samples are recovered — physical observation and laboratory companion testing are not possible.
Probe can be damaged or destroyed in dense/stiff/hard soils if operator is inexperienced.
Specialized equipment and electronic instrumentation typically require a specialty vendor.
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating CPT suitability for a given site or deciding between CPT and other in situ testing methods.

sections.title: Flat Plate Dilatometer
sections.summary: Introduces the flat plate dilatometer test (DMT), standardized in ASTM D6635, which pushes a flat steel blade into the ground in 9- to 12-inch increments and inflates a flexible steel diaphragm. Describes the A (lift-off), B (1.1-mm displacement), and C (optional deflation) membrane pressure readings, and how the DMT can be run from the ground surface or lowered into a borehole. References Figure 2-10.
sections.body: The flat plate dilatometer test (DMT) was developed in Italy and introduced to the United States practice in the 1980s (Marchetti et al. 2006). It has been widely adopted worldwide and the testing procedures have been standardized in ASTM D6635. The test involves pushing a relatively long and thin flat plate into the ground, generally in 9- to 12-inch vertical increments and then inflating a flexible steel diaphragm while making two or three specific measurements (i.e., A, B, and C). The A reading is the pressure required to lift off the membrane from the face of the blade. The B reading is the pressure required to move the center of the membrane a distance of 0.04 inch (1.1 mm) into the soil. The C reading is an optional reading that can be taken by deflating the membrane until the center of the membrane again contacts the face of the blade. Many practitioners perform the DMT using the same specialized equipment for performing a CPT. In most cases, the test is run without an excavated borehole, so no samples or drill cuttings are produced. However, in some cases, the DMT is lowered into a sampled borehole, advanced approximately 12 inches past the base of the borehole and then inflated as described above. A schematic representation of the test is presented in Figure 2-10.
key_points: DMT standardized in ASTM D6635; developed in Italy and introduced to US practice in the 1980s.
Flat blade pushed in 9- to 12-inch increments; flexible steel diaphragm inflated at each stop.
Three membrane readings: A (lift-off pressure), B (1.1-mm displacement pressure), C (optional deflation reading).
Can be run from ground surface (no borehole) or lowered ~12 inches below base of a sampled borehole.
Often uses the same equipment as CPT; no samples or drill cuttings produced in standard configuration.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting or describing the DMT for in situ measurement of soil stiffness, stress history, and soil type.

sections.title: Equipment, Procedure, and Results
sections.summary: Details DMT equipment specifications (blade dimensions: 95-mm wide, 15-mm thick, 190-mm tall; 60-mm stainless steel membrane) and procedure (pushed at 1–3 cm/s using CPT rig). Describes the three DMT index values derived from reduced readings p0, p1, and u0: Material Index (ID) for soil type, Dilatometer Modulus (ED) for stiffness, and Horizontal Stress Index (KD) for stress history. References Chapter 8 for correlations.
sections.body:
A photograph of the flat plate dilatometer is presented in Figure 2-11(a), and the control unit used to perform the test (i.e., control inflation and deflation of the membrane) is shown in Figure 2-11(b). The dilatometer blade is nominally 3.75-inches (95-mm) wide, 0.60-inches (15-mm) thick, and 7.5-inches (190-mm) tall with a 30° apex angle at the tip. A 2.4-inch (60-mm) diameter stainless steel membrane is used. The membrane is typically 0.008-inches (0.20-mm) thick and requires careful calibration. The control unit uses bottled gas (nitrogen) supply. A CPT rig is often used to push the dilatometer at a rate of about 0.4 to 1.2 inches/second (1 to 3 cm/s). The vertical thrust is typically monitored and recorded during the test.

The DMT method and calculations are summarized in Figure 2-10. For more details about the test procedure, refer to NCHRP (2018). The reduced DMT test results produces three values, p0, p1, and u0, from which the following DMT index values are directly calculated for each test depth:

• Material Index, ID = (p1 - p0) / (p0 - u0), which is used to identify soil type;
• Dilatometer Modulus, ED = 34.7×(p1 - p0) in units of atmospheres, which is a measure of soil stiffness; and
• Horizontal Stress Index, KD = (p1 - p0) / σʹv0, which is used to assess stress history.

These three indices are typically plotted with respect to test depth to develop a near-continuous vertical profile. Similar to the techniques used for the CPT, these directly calculated values are used to estimate important engineering parameters, including strength, compressibility, modulus, lateral earth pressure by semi-empirical correlations. A summary of correlations to the DMT results is presented in Chapter 8.
key_points: Blade dimensions: 95-mm wide, 15-mm thick, 190-mm tall; 30° apex; 60-mm diameter, 0.20-mm thick stainless steel membrane requiring careful calibration.
Pushed at 1–3 cm/s using CPT rig; nitrogen gas supply inflates membrane; vertical thrust monitored.
Three index values calculated from p0, p1, u0: Material Index ID, Dilatometer Modulus ED, and Horizontal Stress Index KD.
ID = (p1 − p0)/(p0 − u0) identifies soil type; ED = 34.7×(p1 − p0) measures stiffness; KD = (p0 − u0)/σ′v0 assesses stress history.
Indices plotted vs. depth for near-continuous vertical profile; used in semi-empirical correlations for strength, compressibility, modulus, and lateral earth pressure.
Detailed correlations to DMT results are presented in Chapter 8.
