sections.applicability: Applies when performing or interpreting DMT results to compute Material Index, Dilatometer Modulus, and Horizontal Stress Index for engineering parameter estimation.

sections.title: Advantages and Limitations
sections.summary: Summarizes DMT advantages and limitations. Advantages include speed, simple maintenance, and unique ability to estimate horizontal stress and stiffness not available from SPT or CPT. Limitations include vulnerability of the thin blade and diaphragm to damage from coarse particles, difficult field calibration, sensitivity to humidity causing erratic signaling, and caution needed when applying DMT correlations directly to design.
sections.body:
The DMT provides multiple advantages. The test can be performed relatively quickly using a variety of insertion equipment. The probe itself is relatively simple to maintain and training is not particularly onerous. It provides some information regarding horizontal stress and stiffness, which the SPT and CPT are unable to provide.

A major limitation of the dilatometer is that the thin blade and particularly, the diaphragm, can be easily damaged when penetrating soil with particles the size of coarse sand or larger. The diaphragm can be replaced, but the break-in and calibration procedures must be performed, and that can often be difficult to do in the field. The specialized equipment needs to be maintained and properly cleaned between tests, as erratic electric signaling has been experienced when humid conditions exist beneath the membrane. Caution should be used when using dilatometer correlations directly for engineering design parameters.
key_points: DMT uniquely provides horizontal stress and stiffness information that SPT and CPT cannot.
Quick to perform with simple maintenance; training requirements are not onerous.
Thin blade and diaphragm are easily damaged in soils with coarse sand-sized or larger particles.
Field calibration after diaphragm replacement is difficult.
Humid conditions beneath the membrane can cause erratic electric signaling.
Caution required when directly applying DMT correlations to engineering design parameters.
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating DMT suitability for a given site, particularly in soils with coarse particles or humid conditions.

sections.title: Dynamic Cone Penetrometer
sections.summary: Introduces the Dynamic Cone Penetrometer (DCP), tracing its evolution from a heavy 1950s SPT-surrogate device to the USACE lightweight DCP standardized in ASTM D6951. Describes the lightweight device's correlation to SPT N values and California Bearing Ratio (CBR) per Webster et al. (1992), and its more widespread use in the US.
sections.body: Like the CPT, the dynamic cone penetrometer (DCP) has seen a historical evolution. In the United States, the device was developed in the late 1950s in the southeastern United States, primarily to confirm near-surface conditions for spread footings and as a potential surrogate for the SPT. This original, heavier DCP correlates closely with the SPT blow count but was not formally standardized. The United States Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) developed a lightweight DCP that correlates to SPT N values and California Bearing Ratio, CBR (Webster et al. 1992). This lightweight device has seen more widespread use and is standardized in ASTM D6951.
key_points: DCP evolved from a heavy 1950s southeastern US device to the standardized USACE lightweight DCP.
USACE lightweight DCP correlates to SPT N values and CBR; standardized in ASTM D6951.
Original heavier DCP correlated closely with SPT blow count but was never formally standardized.
Lightweight DCP has seen more widespread use than the original heavier device.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting the DCP for near-surface subsurface evaluation as a surrogate or supplement to SPT, particularly for compaction assessment or CBR correlation.

sections.title: Equipment, Procedure, and Results
sections.summary: Describes DCP equipment (drop hammer of 17.4 or 10.1 lbs, 60° apex cone, upper and lower shafts, extraction jack) and field procedure (two-person operation, 1-inch seating, incremental hammer drops, penetration recorded to 0.1 inch after each blow). Explains calculation of the DCP Penetration Index (DPI) tabulated vs. depth, with correlations to engineering parameters found in Chapter 8.
sections.body:
A schematic of the lightweight DCP equipment and details of the cone tip are presented in Figure 2-12. A drop hammer (either 17.4 or 10.1 pounds) strikes the anvil to drive in the cone tip. The upper and lower shaft guide the hammer and transmit the driving force to the cone tip. The 60° apex angle cone is at the bottom of the lower shaft. Both fixed and disposable cone tips are available. An extraction jack may be needed to remove the cone and shaft.

The DCP is normally conducted by two people. After seating the cone tip about 1.0 inch, the cone is advanced incrementally by successive drops of the hammer, while holding the device vertical. After each hammer blow, the penetration of the cone is measured and recorded to the nearest 0.1 inch. The test is terminated when a target depth is achieved, when the full length of the lower shaft is embedded, or when the total penetration is less than 0.1 inch/blow for 10 successive hammer blows. The extraction jack is then used to retrieve the embedded shaft/cone.

From the recorded test results, the DCP Penetration Index (DPI) is calculated, and tabulated versus depth. A plot can be developed of the incremental values of DPI versus the cumulative penetration depth, providing an indication of relative stiffness/strength versus depth. Correlations to DCP are found in Chapter 8.
key_points: Drop hammer options: 17.4 lb or 10.1 lb; 60° apex angle cone at base of lower shaft.
Two-person operation; cone seated ~1.0 inch before testing begins; device must be held vertical.
Penetration recorded to nearest 0.1 inch after each hammer blow.
Test terminates at target depth, full shaft embedment, or <0.1 inch/blow for 10 successive blows.
DCP Penetration Index (DPI) tabulated vs. depth; plot of incremental DPI vs. cumulative depth indicates stiffness/strength profile.
DCP correlations to engineering parameters are in Chapter 8; DCP often represents DCP Index in equations.
sections.applicability: Applies when performing or interpreting lightweight DCP testing for near-surface stiffness/strength profiling and correlation to SPT or CBR.

sections.title: Advantages and Limitations
sections.summary: Summarizes DCP advantages and limitations. Key advantages are simplicity, low cost, ease of use, suitability for limited-access sites, ability to serve as compaction acceptance criteria, and easy development of local/regional correlations. Limitations include shallow depth of penetration, critical requirement for shaft verticality, operator experience, and safety hazard from pinch points on the donut-style drop hammer.
sections.body:
The DCP is a simple, low-cost, easy-to-use tool, which is ideal for quick or very low-cost results, or when site access is limited. The results of the DCP can be used as compaction acceptance criteria. It can easily assess stratigraphy, particularly in the delineation of soft and hard layers. The equipment is easy to maintain. Perhaps the biggest advantage is that local and regional correlations can be easily developed and updated as needed.

A significant limitation of the test is the shallow depth of penetration. Verticality of the shafts when driving is critical, and operator experience is valuable. Because a donut-style drop hammer is used, the operator (and helper) need to avoid 'pinch points' between the hammer and anvil.
key_points: DCP is simple, low-cost, and easy to use; ideal for limited-access sites or quick results.
Can serve as compaction acceptance criteria and delineate soft vs. hard layers.
Local and regional correlations can be easily developed and updated.
Major limitation: shallow depth of penetration.
Shaft verticality during driving is critical; operator experience is important.
Safety hazard: donut-style drop hammer creates pinch points between hammer and anvil.
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating DCP suitability for a project, particularly regarding shallow near-surface conditions, site access constraints, or compaction verification.

sections.title: GROUNDWATER MEASUREMENTS
sections.summary: Covers the principles and methods for locating and monitoring the groundwater table during subsurface investigations, including how water levels are recorded during drilling, the role of piezometers, interpretation challenges (perched/confined water, gradients, transient conditions), and the distinction between steady-state and transient pore pressure monitoring.
sections.body:
Because of its importance in geotechnical analysis, location of the groundwater table is a key element of a subsurface investigation. During drilling, depths are typically recorded at which the water is first encountered in the borehole and at which the water level stabilizes after drilling. The latter is often recorded after the borehole remains open for approximately 24 hours. In some soils, the sidewalls will collapse unless they are confined or supported (e.g., sands beneath the water table). In these cases, perforated pipe may be used as a temporary casing to protect against borehole collapse while allowing water to flow through the perforations. Knowledge of the seasonal groundwater fluctuation is important, and long-term measurements can be made by converting borings to piezometers, which can vary from open wells to electronic transducers.

Knowledge of the local groundwater regime is required to correctly interpret groundwater measurements, especially those from piezometers. Groundwater can occur at different elevations in the subsurface. It may be perched in isolated zones, or it may be confined between different low-permeability strata. In addition, groundwater flow can affect the interpretation of water levels. Where gradients are low and the groundwater table is relatively horizontal, groundwater depths can be directly inferred from piezometer measurements. However, where large gradients are present, the water pressure measured at a point in the ground cannot be directly used to calculate the vertical depth of water above that point. Knowledge of the seepage conditions is required (see Chapter 7-6) to make this determination. Finally, a distinction must be made between steady state and transient conditions. Steady state conditions can be effectively monitored using all types of piezometers. However, under transient conditions (e.g., rapid drawdown in dams, consolidation or swell in fine-grained soils), pore pressures may be changing significantly with time and require instrumentation with a fast response time, such as diaphragm type transducers.
key_points: Water level is recorded both when first encountered and after stabilization (~24 hours after drilling).
Perforated temporary casing may be needed in sands below the water table to prevent borehole collapse.
Borings can be converted to piezometers for long-term seasonal groundwater monitoring.
Perched or confined groundwater requires careful local regime knowledge to correctly interpret piezometer readings.
Where large hydraulic gradients exist, measured water pressure cannot be directly converted to depth without seepage analysis.
Transient conditions (rapid drawdown, consolidation) require fast-response instruments such as diaphragm-type transducers.
sections.applicability: Applies to all subsurface investigations where groundwater table location and pore pressure conditions must be determined.

sections.title: Types of Standpipe Piezometer
sections.summary: Introduces the three common types of standpipe piezometers used for groundwater level monitoring — open well, open standpipe, and porous element — and identifies the three basic components (tip/screen, standpipe, seal). References Figure 2-13 and Table 2-17 for depictions and comparisons of types.
sections.body:
Groundwater level monitoring involves direct measurement of water levels within open well, open standpipe piezometer, or porous element piezometers. The common types of standpipe piezometer for monitoring groundwater levels are depicted in Figure 2-13 and summarized in Table 2-17. The type of standpipe that is selected depends on preferences, regulations (if applicable), and the type of subsurface soils in which the groundwater level will be measured.

The three basic components of a standpipe piezometer include: (1) the tip or well screen; (2) the standpipe itself; and (3) the standpipe seal. These can be installed by hand at shallow depths, but in most cases are installed using a drill rig after the completion of a boring in the soil or rock.
key_points: Three main standpipe piezometer types: open well, open standpipe, and porous element.
All standpipe piezometers share three components: tip/screen, standpipe, and seal.
Selection depends on site regulations, soil type, and monitoring objectives.
Most installations use a drill rig after boring completion; hand installation is possible only at shallow depths.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting a piezometer type for groundwater level monitoring during geotechnical site investigations.

sections.title: Open Well Piezometer
sections.summary: Describes the open well piezometer, which uses a full-length perforated screen and filter sand backfill in an open boring. Best suited for homogeneous, high-permeability deposits. Used widely for environmental groundwater sampling. Explains that water level reflects the stratum with the highest total head when multiple strata are crossed.
sections.body:
A common groundwater monitoring technique is to install a standpipe, or water tight pipe, within an open boring as shown in Figure 2-13(a). The standpipe has a perforated tip or screen that allows water to enter are usually small-diameter (e.g., less than 2 inches) PVC plastic pipe but may be larger for environmental sampling applications. In an open well, the annular space between the pipe and borehole wall is filled with filter sand or gravel almost to the ground surface. At the ground surface, a seal of cement grout, bentonite slurry, or other low permeability material is placed above the filter sand to isolate the well from surface water flow. Open wells are often called groundwater monitoring wells and are commonly used for environmental applications when samples of the groundwater are required.

Because an open well has a full-length screen or a full depth filter zone, it is best suited for measuring water levels in relatively homogeneous deposits with high permeability. When multiple strata are crossed, the groundwater level corresponds to the stratum with the highest total head. A significant advantage of an open well piezometer is that it can be cleaned and 'developed' by flushing water from the standpipe into the formation, which is critical for open well piezometers used for environmental applications.
key_points: Open well uses a full-length screen and filter sand/gravel backfill along the entire borehole annulus.
Typically small-diameter (<2 inches) PVC pipe; larger diameters may be used for environmental sampling.
Surface seal (cement grout or bentonite) isolates the well from surface water infiltration.
Best suited for homogeneous, high-permeability soils; in layered profiles, reads the highest total-head stratum.
Can be developed by flushing, making it ideal for environmental groundwater sampling applications.
sections.applicability: Applies when monitoring groundwater in homogeneous, high-permeability soils or when groundwater sampling for environmental purposes is required.

sections.title: Open Standpipe Piezometer
sections.summary: Describes the open standpipe piezometer, which differs from an open well by isolating a specific stratum with seals above and below the screen zone. Explains nested piezometer installations for measuring multiple strata in a single borehole and discusses the equalization time limitation, including the option to reduce pipe diameter to below 0.5 inches to speed response.
sections.body:
An open standpipe piezometer is similar to an open well, except that the screen extends only across a specific stratum of interest. Seals are installed above and below this zone to only allow water to enter from the stratum of interest. An open standpipe piezometer is shown in Figure 2-13(b). Outside of the screened test section, select backfill materials are used but not necessarily filter sand. A seal is typically placed around the open standpipe at the ground surface.

Multiple open standpipe piezometers can be installed to measure groundwater levels in multiple strata within a single borehole through careful installation of multiple seals. This approach is sometimes referred to as a nested piezometer. The vertical location (i.e., depth, thickness, and elevation) of each seal must be accurately measured and recorded on the well log.

A major disadvantage of open well and open standpipe piezometers is the long equalization time that may be required for water to flow from the formation and fill the piezometer. Until the groundwater level stabilizes in this manner, the readings are inaccurate. To reduce the equalization time, the diameter of the standpipe can be reduced to less than 0.5 inches, which decreases the volume of water needed.
key_points: Screen is limited to a specific stratum of interest, with seals above and below to isolate the measurement zone.
Nested piezometers allow multiple strata to be monitored within a single borehole using multiple seals.
Seal depth, thickness, and elevation must be accurately recorded on the well log.
Long equalization time is a key disadvantage; reducing standpipe diameter to <0.5 inches mitigates this.
Backfill outside the screened zone need not be filter sand.
sections.applicability: Applies when groundwater levels must be measured in a discrete stratum or in multiple distinct strata within a single borehole.

sections.title: Porous Element Piezometers
sections.summary: Describes porous element (hydraulic) piezometers, which use a ceramic or porous metal tip with pore sizes <50 microns attached to a small-diameter riser pipe. Key advantage is shorter equalization time in fine-grained, low-permeability soils compared to open well or standpipe types, though water still must flow through the element into the standpipe for accurate readings.
sections.body: The primary disadvantage of open well and open standpipe piezometers is the potentially long equalization time for the groundwater level to stabilize since the riser pipe must fill with a considerable volume of water from the formation. Porous element or hydraulic piezometers have a ceramic or porous metal tip attached to a small-diameter riser pipe (i.e., standpipe). Modern versions use a porous element with pore sizes of <50 microns, so that the tip can be used in direct contact with fine-grained soils. One of the primary advantages of the porous element piezometer is the relatively short equalization time periods in fine-grained soils exhibiting low permeability. However, water must still flow from the formation through the porous element and into the standpipe to obtain accurate groundwater level measurements.
key_points: Uses a ceramic or porous metal tip with pore sizes <50 microns, enabling use in fine-grained soils.
Primary advantage over open well/standpipe types is significantly shorter equalization time in low-permeability soils.
Water must still flow through the porous element into the standpipe for accurate readings.
Comes in hydraulic (porous element) and electronic variants, each with different advantages and limitations per Table 2-17.
sections.applicability: Applies when monitoring groundwater in fine-grained, low-permeability soils where fast response time is needed.

sections.title: Multiple or Nested Installations
sections.summary: Explains nested piezometer installations where multiple standpipe piezometers are placed in a single boring separated by impervious seals, reducing borehole numbers and construction obstacles. Notes that when measurement zones are within 10 feet of vertical separation, separate borings are required for reliable results.
sections.body: Several standpipe piezometers may be installed in a single boring with an impervious seal separating the different measuring zones. These are called nested piezometers. This concept represents a cost advantage, as it reduces the number of borings (but increases the difficulties/challenges of installing seals and specific elevations) and the number of 'obstacles' during for the contractor during construction. However, if measurements are needed in zones with 10 feet or less of vertical separation, piezometers should be installed in separate borings.
key_points: Nested piezometers use impervious seals to isolate multiple measurement zones within a single boring.
Cost-effective approach that reduces total number of borings and construction obstacles.
Increases installation complexity due to the need for precise seal placement at correct elevations.
When vertical separation between zones is 10 feet or less, separate borings are required.
sections.applicability: Applies when groundwater levels in multiple strata must be monitored while minimizing the number of boreholes drilled.

sections.title: Measurement of Groundwater Levels
sections.summary: Describes direct and indirect methods for measuring groundwater levels in standpipe piezometers. Direct methods include surveying riser pipe elevation, measuring stick-up, and measuring depth to water using tapes or electrical indicators (±0.5 inch accuracy). Indirect methods use submerged pressure transducers, enabling automated data collection required for pumping tests and in situ permeability calculations. Covers limitations including lag time, access issues, precipitation entry, and gas bubbles.
sections.body:
Groundwater levels/elevations can be obtained by either direct or indirect methods. The direct method includes: (1) surveying the elevation of the top of the riser pipe and/or the ground surface; (2) measuring or calculating the 'stick-up' of the riser pipe above the ground surface; and (3) measuring the distance depth from the top of the riser pipe to the water surface inside the open pipe or the standpipe. The elevation of the groundwater can then be easily calculated. There are several methods to measure the distance from the water surface to the top of the riser pipe; including a plumb bob, cloth or metal surveyors' tapes coated with chalk, or commercially available electrical indicators. Using these direct measurements, the water level can be established generally within a tolerance of about 0.5 inch.

An indirect, but more accurate, method for measuring the depth of water in an open well uses an electrical transducer capable of measuring water pressure. The transducer is attached to a hoisting cable and an electrical cable. Markings on the electrical cable are used to measure the length of the cable in the open pipe. Commercially, these portable systems are called water level indicators. The transducer is lowered to a depth typically near the bottom of the open hole such that the transducer is submerged. The electrical cable is attached at the surface to a readout unit that measures the pressure due to water column above the tip of the transducer. From the unit weight of water (i.e., 62.4 pcf or 9.81 kN/m3), the depth of water above the tip of the transducer is calculated, which combined with the length of cable in the open pipe can be used to calculate the groundwater level in the pipe. This type of transducer can be connected to a data collection unit and groundwater levels can be automatically collected over time. This capability is often quite efficient and is, in fact, a requirement when groundwater pumping tests are performed and the time-dependent groundwater elevation as a function of pumping rate is necessary for subsequent calculations of in situ permeability of a formation (see Section 2-9.2). The indirect method can also be used with pore pressure transducers that are grouted or sealed directly in boreholes without a standpipe. More information on the transducers used with this type of piezometer is provided in Section 2-10.4.

While being simple in concept, the techniques for measuring groundwater levels have some inherent limitations. First, standpipe piezometers require access to the top of the vertical riser pipe, which usually extends above the ground surface and may be easily damaged during construction. If the riser is extended vertically during construction (e.g., installed in a constructed embankment), the extension activities must be carefully coordinated with the earthwork contractor. Manual or direct measurement of water levels is time consuming and may adversely impact construction. The largest source of error for standpipe piezometers is the lag time required for the piezometer to respond to changing groundwater levels because water must flow from the formation into the piezometer. For this reason, groundwater piezometers are intended to measure hydrostatic groundwater levels and are inappropriate for time-dependent pore pressures. Other sources of error that impact piezometer readings include the possibility of direct introduction of precipitation into the riser pipe due to a missing or vandalized cap, infiltration of surface water into the borehole, and the formation of gas bubbles within the pipe. Indirect groundwater measurements by porous element piezometers without a standpipe or pore pressure transducers can alleviate many of these limitations.
key_points: Direct methods (tapes, chalk-coated tapes, plumb bob, electrical indicators) achieve ~0.5-inch accuracy.
Indirect method uses a submerged pressure transducer (water level indicator) with unit weight of water (62.4 pcf / 9.81 kN/m³) to calculate depth.
Automated transducer data collection is required for groundwater pumping tests used to calculate in situ permeability.
Largest error source in standpipe piezometers is lag time; they are unsuitable for measuring time-dependent pore pressures.
Other error sources: precipitation entry through damaged cap, surface water infiltration, gas bubble formation.
Porous element piezometers and grouted pore pressure transducers (Section 2-10.4) can overcome many standpipe limitations.
sections.applicability: Applies whenever groundwater levels are measured in standpipe or porous element piezometers during geotechnical investigation or construction monitoring.

sections.title: Detection of Combustible Gases
sections.summary: Addresses the hazard of combustible gases — primarily methane (CH4) and carbon dioxide (CO2) — in subsurface soils at sites near landfills, peat bogs, marshes, or swamp deposits. Explains that methane is produced by anaerobic decomposition of organic material and that portable landfill gas analyzers are used to detect gas presence and concentration in wells and borings above the water table.
sections.body: Gas bubbles in groundwater can influence the measurement of groundwater levels. Gas can exist in subsurface soils and pose other hazards. Specifically, methane (CH4) and other combustible gases may be present in subsurface soils and rock, particularly in sites near municipal solid waste (MSW) landfills, or at sites near or over peat bogs, marshes, and swamp deposits. Methane is a dominating combustible gas in the subsurface because it is one of the primary by-products of the anaerobic decomposition of organic material. The other dominant gas is carbon dioxide (CO2). Commercially available portable instruments, referenced as landfill gas analyzers, are used to detect the presence and concentration of combustible methane gas in landfill gas wells and monitoring probes. These instruments sample the air/gas from the confined space in wells and borings above the water table.
key_points: Gas bubbles in groundwater can distort piezometer readings and pose safety hazards.
Methane (CH4) is the primary combustible subsurface gas, produced by anaerobic decomposition of organics.
CO2 is the other dominant gas; both are found near MSW landfills, peat bogs, marshes, and swamps.
Portable landfill gas analyzers sample air/gas from confined spaces in wells and borings above the water table to detect concentration.
sections.applicability: Applies at sites near MSW landfills, peat bogs, marshes, or swamp deposits where combustible subsurface gases may be present.

sections.title: Measurement of Soil and Rock Properties In Situ
sections.summary: Introduces in situ testing as a complement or replacement to field sampling and laboratory testing. Covers the growing use of in situ methods since the 1980s, highlights SPT, CPT, DMT, and DCP as popular correlation-based tools, and outlines the scope of this section: strength, stiffness/modulus, permeability, as-compacted earthwork properties, and rock testing methods.
sections.body:
Field sampling and laboratory testing can sometimes be complemented or replaced by in situ testing, which refers to measurements conducted on soil and rock "in place." As a general rule, an in situ testing program can be performed faster and in many cases at a lower cost than most laboratory testing programs. As a result, this alternative has seen growing popularity since the 1980s. The SPT, CPT, DMT, and DCP are four of the most popular in situ testing methods, which are often correlated to engineering parameters. This section discusses other in situ tests that measure strength, stiffness/modulus, and permeability of existing soils, as well as the as compacted properties of earthwork. Methods for in situ testing of rock are also discussed.

Although not universally adopted, many practitioners find that the pocket penetrometer and the field torvane provide useful correlations to the shear strength as measured in the laboratory. These tests may be performed on the soil exposed at the bottom of a recovered Shelby tube sample. Practitioners who use these tests often correlate the results to results from laboratory strength tests, to increase the value of the field test. Although these tests are often used in practice, the results are very inexact and should not be used for design.
key_points: In situ testing is generally faster and lower cost than laboratory testing programs.
SPT, CPT, DMT, and DCP are the most popular in situ testing methods correlated to engineering parameters.
Pocket penetrometer and field torvane provide useful but inexact shear strength correlations; should not be used for design.
Section covers strength, stiffness/modulus, permeability, as-compacted earthwork, and rock in situ testing methods.
sections.applicability: Applies when planning geotechnical investigations where in situ testing may complement or replace laboratory testing.

sections.title: Strength and Deformation Properties of Soil
sections.summary: Introduces the three most commonly used in situ testing methods for assessing strength and stiffness of soils: pressuremeter test (PMT), vane shear test (VST), and plate load test (PLT). Directs the reader to Table 2-18, which summarizes and compares these tests including applicable soil types, measurable properties, limitations, and relevant ASTM standards.
sections.body: The pressuremeter test, vane shear test, and the plate load test are the most commonly used in situ testing methods for assessing strength and stiffness of soils. A summary and comparison of these tests is presented in Table 2-18. Where ASTM standards are available, they have been included in the table.
key_points: PMT, VST, and PLT are the three primary in situ tests for soil strength and deformation.
Table 2-18 summarizes procedures, applicable soil types, measurable properties, and limitations for each test.

Measurable properties include elastic modulus (E), shear modulus (G), undrained shear strength (su), sensitivity (St), preconsolidation stress (σ'p), ultimate bearing capacity (qult), and modulus of subgrade reaction (ks).
ASTM standards D4719, D2573, and D1196 apply to PMT, VST, and PLT respectively.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting in situ testing methods to evaluate strength and deformation properties of soils.

sections.title: Pressuremeter Test
sections.summary: Describes the pressuremeter test (PMT), developed ~1955, in which a membrane is inflated against borehole sidewalls to calculate strength and deformation properties. Covers equipment, test procedure per ASTM D4719, characteristic pressure-volume curve, and variants including the pre-bored (Menard), self-boring (SBPMT), and full-displacement (CPMT) pressuremeters.
sections.body:
The pressuremeter test (PMT) was first developed in about 1955. In the PMT, a membrane is inflated from a cylindrical probe against the sidewalls of an open borehole. The radial expansion is measured, and this response is used to calculate specific strength and deformation properties of the subsurface soils. PMT can be performed in a wide range of materials, including sands, residual soil, tills, and soft rock, that are usually difficult to sample. The "traditional" is called the "pre-bored" or "Menard" pressuremeter. Other types include the self-boring pressuremeter (SBPMT) that includes its own cutting shoe and does not require an existing borehole and the full-displacement or cone pressuremeter (CPMT) that is pushed into the ground, usually behind a piezocone.

The equipment needed to perform a PMT includes an expandable cylindrical probe, rubber membrane, outer slotted sleeve, pressure lines, and control unit. The PMT procedures are defined in ASTM D4719. The inner membrane is hydraulically expanded to obtain an expansion pressure versus volume curve. During loading, disturbed soil in the borehole wall first compresses, followed by a pseudo-elastic response and then plastic yielding. After plastic yielding is induced, a creep test is performed by holding pressure constant until the lateral expansion falls below a threshold. The PMT concludes with an unload-reload cycle to better define the elastic properties.
key_points: Three PMT variants: pre-bored (Menard), self-boring (SBPMT), and full-displacement/cone (CPMT).
Applicable to sands, residual soils, tills, and soft rock that are difficult to sample.
Test procedure per ASTM D4719 produces an expansion pressure vs. volume curve with three phases: compression, pseudo-elastic, and plastic yielding.
Unload-reload cycle at end of test is used to better define elastic properties.
SBPMT eliminates the need for an existing borehole and reduces disturbance-related errors.
sections.applicability: Applies when conducting in situ testing of strength and deformation in soils difficult to sample, using borehole-based or push-in pressuremeter equipment.

sections.title: Test Interpretation
sections.summary: Covers interpretation of PMT results for three parameters: coefficient of lateral earth pressure at rest (K0), soil stiffness (via pressuremeter modulus Ep or shear modulus G from cavity expansion theory), and undrained shear strength (su). Notes that K0 accuracy is questionable for the pre-bored PMT and that su estimates from PMT are less reliable than from CPT or VST.
sections.body:
Pressuremeter tests have been used to estimate the coefficient of lateral earth pressure at rest (K0), the soil stiffness; and undrained shear strength (su).

• Coefficient of Lateral Earth Pressure at Rest (K0): Upon initial inflation, the membrane will expand to contact the borehole sidewalls. In the PMT, p0 is related to the in situ total horizontal stress, which combined with the vertical stress allows K0 to be calculated. Due to unloading effects and disturbance during drilling the borehole, the accuracy of this calculation is questionable. To accurately assess the in situ lateral stress and K0, a self-boring pressuremeter should be considered. Point A in Figure 2-16 is a relatively accurate representation of the total horizontal stress in the ground.

• Stiffness: The elastic stiffness of the soil can be estimated by the slope of the unload-reload pressuremeter curve where the response is assumed to be nearly elastic. One technique calculates the pressuremeter modulus (Ep), while another uses cavity expansion theory to calculate shear modulus, G (Gibson and Anderson 1961, Windle and Wroth 1977).

• Undrained Shear Strength (su): Methods exist to estimate the undrained shear strength from pressuremeter results, but the resulting values are less reliable than those from other in situ tests, such as the cone penetration test or the vane shear test.
key_points: PMT p0 is related to in situ total horizontal stress, but K0 calculation from pre-bored PMT is unreliable due to drilling disturbance.
SBPMT provides more accurate K0 and in situ lateral stress estimates.
Soil stiffness is estimated from the unload-reload curve slope; Ep or G (via cavity expansion theory) can be calculated.
su from PMT is less reliable than from CPT or VST.
sections.applicability: Applies when interpreting pressuremeter test results for K0, stiffness, or undrained shear strength of soils.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.summary: Describes the key limitations of pressuremeter testing including sensitivity to borehole stability (especially in soft soils and sands), effects of borehole wall irregularities, the need for specialist operators for SBPMT, the theoretical requirement for drained or undrained conditions, probe length averaging effects in stratified soils, and equipment maintenance demands.
sections.body: Pressuremeter testing is sensitive to test procedures. In very soft soils and in sands, it may be difficult to maintain borehole stability before the probe is inserted. In these cases, a self-boring pressuremeter may be necessary. Irregularities in the wall of the borehole wall also affects test results, and the self-boring pressuremeter eliminates some of this disadvantage. The SBPMT usually requires a specialist familiar with the test and the instrument. Pressuremeter test interpretation has a theoretical basis and, therefore, either drained or undrained conditions need to be maintained. The pressuremeter is relatively long (i.e., generally greater than 2 feet in length) and results reflect an averaging of the soils over this length. For this reason, the PMT in best used in relatively homogenous deposits, and it not expected to provide reliable parameters in stratified soil. Pressuremeter equipment has many moving parts and requires maintenance and careful handling.
key_points: Borehole stability is critical; SBPMT required in very soft soils or sands.
Borehole wall irregularities degrade test results; SBPMT reduces this problem.
SBPMT requires a specialist operator.
Drained or undrained conditions must be maintained during testing for valid interpretation.
PMT probe length (>2 ft) averages soil response; unreliable in stratified deposits.
Equipment has many moving parts requiring regular maintenance and careful handling.
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating the suitability and limitations of pressuremeter testing for a specific site or soil condition.

sections.title: Vane Shear Test
sections.summary: Describes the vane shear test (VST), in use since the 1940s, for measuring undrained shear strength and sensitivity of soft to stiff clays and silts. Provides equations for undrained shear strength (Eq. 2-1), sensitivity (Eq. 2-2), and the vane-corrected field shear strength (Eq. 2-3) using correction factor µR. Notes limitations including inapplicability in fissured clays, gravelly soils, and laminated soils.
sections.body:
The vane shear test (VST) is a popular and reliable in situ test that has been in use since the 1940s. The VST involves the use of a simple four-sided blade (i.e., vane) that is pushed into the ground and then rotated to evaluate the undrained shear strength and sensitivity of soft to stiff clays and silts. The use of the VST should be limited to soils in which slow (i.e., ~6° / min) rotation of the vane represents undrained shearing. At failure, the vane will cut a "cylinder" of soil equivalent to the outside dimensions of the vane and the torque will reduce. The vane is often rotated 10 more revolutions, and the residual torque is measured.

The undrained shear strength (su,fv), the remolded undrained shear strength (sur,fv), and the sensitivity (St,fv), can be obtained from the VST. During rotation, the maximum net torque (Tmax) is measured and the undrained shear strength for a "standard" rectangular vane with an H/D ratio of 2 is given by Equation 2-1. To measure the remolded undrained shear strength, the torque reading (Tres) is taken during rotation of the vane following five to ten rapid turns, and the remolded strength is calculated by replacing Tmax with Tres in Equation 2-1. Sensitivity is calculated by Equation 2-2.

The undrained shear strength from the VST overpredicts the shear strength mobilized in failures of embankments, shallow footings, and slopes constructed on soft clay. In order to account for this, su,fv should be adjusted by a correction factor (µR), which is a function of the PI of the soil tested. Three different vane correction methods are given in the ASTM specification. The corrected shear strength is calculated by Equation 2-3.

The VST has proven to be a very reliable and repeatable in situ test and enjoys widespread popularity due to cost and efficiency. It is perhaps the best device to measure the in situ strength of soft to medium clays (su < 2000 psf). The biggest limitation of the VST is the types of soil where it can be used. The VST cannot accurately assess the strength of fissured clays, clays with significant amounts of sand or gravel, and soils with relatively thin laminations. The data for the VST is reduced based on the assumption of undrained conditions. Therefore, soils that might allow partial drainage during shear are problematic.
key_points: VST measures undrained shear strength (su,fv), remolded shear strength (sur,fv), and sensitivity (St,fv) using maximum and residual torque.
Eq. 2-1 computes su,fv from maximum torque Tmax for a standard rectangular vane (H/D = 2).
Eq. 2-2 computes sensitivity as ratio of peak to remolded undrained shear strength.
VST overpredicts strength for embankment/footing/slope failures; correction factor µR (function of PI) applied per Eq. 2-3.
Best suited for soft to medium clays (su < 2000 psf); ASTM D2573.
Not suitable for fissured clays, gravelly clays, thinly laminated soils, or soils prone to partial drainage during shear.

equations.description: Undrained shear strength from vane shear test for a standard rectangular vane (H/D = 2): su,fv = 6*Tmax / (7*π*D³)
Sensitivity from vane shear test: St,fv = su,fv / sur,fv (ratio of peak to remolded undrained shear strength)
Corrected field undrained shear strength: su,field = µR × su,fv, where µR is the vane correction factor (function of PI)

sections.applicability: Applies when measuring undrained shear strength and sensitivity of soft to stiff clays and silts using the in situ vane shear test.

sections.title: Hydraulic Conductivity of Soil
sections.summary: Covers in situ measurement of hydraulic conductivity, which spans more than ten orders of magnitude and is highly sensitive to soil type, disturbance, stratigraphy, and variability. Identifies five physical characteristics influencing test performance, emphasizes the importance of isolating uniform zones, and summarizes four common in situ hydraulic conductivity test types in Table 2-19 (constant head, variable head, pressure, and pumping tests).
sections.body:
Hydraulic conductivity is the most variable of all the material properties commonly measured and used in geotechnical analysis, with the range extending to more than ten orders of magnitude. Accurate measurement of hydraulic conductivity is very sensitive to the type of soil, the disturbance of the soil, site stratigraphy, and the variability of the soil deposit across the site. Laboratory testing of the hydraulic conductivity of soil, even on samples of minimally disturbed recovered samples, may not reflect the hydraulic conductivity of the natural deposit because the lab sample is quite small and certainly not representative of a geologically placed and weathered material. If the soils at the site are relatively uniform and can be sampled with minimal disturbance (i.e., uniform clay soils), laboratory testing may be sufficient and adequate. However, for deposits of coarse-grained materials, intact samples are nearly impossible to obtain, and in situ hydraulic conductivity tests are commonly used. In particular, in situ tests are important for uniform coarse-grained deposits. Correlations based on grain-size distribution are also very common for coarse-grained deposits (see Chapter 8).

The following five physical characteristics influence the performance and applicability of in situ hydraulic conductivity tests: (1) water level position, (2) type of soil or rock, (3) depth of the test zone, (4) hydraulic conductivity of the test zone, and (5) heterogeneity and anisotropy of the test zone.

The difficulties inherent with in situ hydraulic conductivity testing require that great care be taken to minimize sources of error and to correctly interpret and compensate for deviations from ideal test conditions. Many of these difficulties can be overcome by planning tests to isolate specific zones of material assumed to be uniform.

In situ hydraulic conductivity tests are most commonly used in geotechnical engineering investigations for dams, hydraulic barriers, geo-environmental projects, and projects with a strong hydrogeologic component. For strictly geotechnical applications, steady-state testing is much more common than transient state testing. In addition, saturated hydraulic conductivity testing is more common than in situ testing for unsaturated conditions. A brief summary of the four most common types of in situ hydraulic conductivity tests is presented in Table 2-19.

A considerable amount of skill is necessary to correctly measure the hydraulic conductivity of soil in situ. Specialty firms will likely provide more accurate and prompt results compared with the personnel used for routine drilling and sampling.
key_points: Hydraulic conductivity spans more than ten orders of magnitude and is highly sensitive to soil type, disturbance, and site variability.
Five factors influence in situ test performance: water level, soil/rock type, test depth, hydraulic conductivity of test zone, and heterogeneity/anisotropy.
In situ tests are especially important for coarse-grained deposits where intact sampling is not feasible.
Four common test types: constant head, variable head (rising/falling), pressure tests, and pumping tests (Table 2-19).
Steady-state and saturated hydraulic conductivity testing dominate for geotechnical applications.
Specialty firms with hydrogeologists recommended for accurate in situ permeability testing.
sections.applicability: Applies when designing or conducting in situ hydraulic conductivity testing for geotechnical investigations involving dams, barriers, or hydrogeologic assessments.

sections.title: Engineered Fill and Earthworks
sections.summary: Introduces measurement of as-compacted moisture content and unit weight for compacted soils in engineered fills and earthworks (dams, embankments). Explains that compaction water content is more critical for fine-grained soils, highlights the importance of both parameters for engineering properties, and notes emerging use of stiffness-measuring compactors that are supplanting traditional QC methods.
sections.body:
The as-compacted moisture/water content and unit weight (often referred to as density) of compacted soils is a significant component of geotechnical practice involving constructed engineered fill or earthworks (e.g., dams, embankments, etc.). For purposes of this discussion, the terms moisture content and unit weight will be used. Geotechnical engineers have long recognized that many of the desired engineering properties of both fine- and coarse-grained compacted materials depend on the compaction moisture content and/or unit weight. The compaction water content is much more important for fine-grained as opposed to coarse-grained soils. This section focuses on the use and limitations of the numerous techniques used in practice for these important measurements.

It should be noted that compactors are currently available that can measure the stiffness of soils "on-the-fly" during compaction (McGuire et al. 2009). These special compactors are becoming very popular in earthwork construction, and their use has supplanted many of the older methods of compaction quality control incorporated into earthwork specifications.
key_points: As-compacted moisture content and unit weight are critical quality control parameters for engineered fill and earthworks.
Compaction water content is more important for fine-grained soils than coarse-grained soils.
Modern compactors can measure soil stiffness on-the-fly during compaction, increasingly replacing traditional QC methods.
Section covers four general strategies for unit weight and multiple methods for moisture content measurement.
sections.applicability: Applies when specifying or performing quality control measurements for compacted engineered fill or earthwork construction.

sections.title: Measurement of As-Compacted Soil Unit Weight
sections.summary: Introduces four general strategies for assessing as-compacted unit weight: displacement methods, drive-cylinder methods, nuclear gauge methods, and non-nuclear gauge methods. All methods assess near-surface characteristics from the ground surface. Notes that total unit weight is measured and water content must be separately determined to compute dry unit weight.
sections.body: Four general strategies can be used to assess the as-compacted unit weight of soils: (1) displacement methods; (2) drive-cylinder methods; and (3) nuclear gauge methods; and (4) non-nuclear gauge methods. All of these methods use measurements from the ground surface to assess the near-surface characteristics of the soil. This section provides a discussion of each of these strategies and methods.
key_points: Four strategies for as-compacted unit weight: displacement, drive-cylinder, nuclear gauge, and non-nuclear gauge methods.
All methods assess near-surface soil characteristics from the ground surface.
All displacement and drive-cylinder methods measure total unit weight; separate water content determination is needed for dry unit weight.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting a method to measure as-compacted unit weight of soils in earthwork quality control.

sections.title: Displacement Methods
sections.summary: Describes sand cone (ASTM D1556) and water balloon displacement (ASTM D2167) methods for measuring in situ total unit weight. Both methods excavate a known weight of soil and use sand or water to measure hole volume. The sand cone is the recognized reference test; the water balloon method should not be used in gravelly soils due to puncture risk.
sections.body:
Of the displacement methods, the sand displacement and water balloon displacement techniques are the most widely used because of their simplicity, applicability to a wide range of material types, and their historical performance and record of accuracy. In both cases, a known weight of soil is excavated from the ground. Either sand or water of a known unit weight is used to measure the volume of the excavated hole. The results are more accurate when a large volume is measured. Displacement methods measure the total unit weight of the soil. The water content of the excavated soil must be determined to calculate the dry unit weight.

The sand displacement method, usually referenced as the "sand cone" method, is the most frequently used displacement test to assess in situ dry unit weight. Originally standardized in 1958 (ASTM D1556), the sand cone method remains the recognized reference test for all other methods used to assess in situ soil unit weight. Consistent results strongly depend on operator experience and care in performing the test.

The water balloon displacement test (ASTM D2167) uses the same principle as the sand cone. The excavated hole in the soil is lined with a balloon (i.e., watertight, thin membrane), which is filled with pressurized water from a volume-calibrated container. The water balloon method should not be used in soils that contain significant amounts of gravel that can potentially puncture the balloon. The water balloon method generally provides consistent and accurate results when performed correctly, although not as consistent as the sand cone (Berney et al. 2013).
key_points: Sand cone (ASTM D1556, standardized 1958) is the recognized reference test for all other in situ unit weight methods.
Water balloon displacement (ASTM D2167) uses the same principle but should not be used in gravelly soils due to balloon puncture risk.
Both methods measure total unit weight; separate water content test needed for dry unit weight.
Larger excavation volume improves accuracy of displacement methods.
Sand cone results depend heavily on operator experience and care.
sections.applicability: Applies when measuring in situ total or dry unit weight of compacted soils using displacement-based methods during earthwork quality control.

sections.title: Drive-Cylinder Method
sections.summary: Describes the drive-cylinder method (ASTM D2937), a rapid technique using a slide hammer to drive a thin-walled tube into the ground to obtain a sample for total unit weight measurement. The method is limited to fine-grained soils or moist fine sands with apparent cohesion; cannot be used in gravelly soils. Separate water content determination is needed for dry unit weight.
sections.body: The drive cylinder method (ASTM D2937) is a convenient and rapid technique to obtain the as-compacted total unit weight of soil. A slide hammer is used to drive a relatively short thin-walled tube (e.g., shortened Shelby tube) into the ground to obtain a sample. After the cylinder is driven, the soil-filled cylinder is carefully dug out of the ground, and the top and bottom of the sample is trimmed flush with the ends of the tube. The inside volume of the tube is the volume of the sample. This method can be used as long as the soil will remain in the cylinder, most notably fine-grained soils containing little or no gravel and moist, fine sands that exhibit apparent cohesion. The method cannot be used in soils that contain gravel, as the cylinder can be easily damaged. The drive cylinder measures the total unit weight, and the water content must be determined by drying the soil sample.
key_points: ASTM D2937; uses a slide hammer and thin-walled tube driven into the ground.
Tube inside volume equals sample volume; convenient and rapid.
Limited to fine-grained soils and moist fine sands with apparent cohesion.
Cannot be used in gravelly soils — cylinder damage risk.
Measures total unit weight; separate drying step required for dry unit weight.
sections.applicability: Applies when rapidly measuring as-compacted total unit weight of fine-grained soils or moist fine sands during earthwork quality control.

sections.title: Nuclear Gauge Method
sections.summary: Describes the nuclear gauge method (ASTM D6938) for measuring soil unit weight and moisture content using gamma ray emission (typically Cesium-231). Explains the direct transmission mode, the importance of regular calibration, and NRC safety requirements (NUREG/BR-0133) including operator training and dosimeter use.
sections.body:
The use of nuclear technology to assess soil unit weight and moisture content commenced in the early 1950s (Burgers and Yoder 1962). The nuclear source (usually Cesium-231) is housed near the tip of a rod that is inserted in a prepared hole at the test location. A low-power nuclear source is used to emit gamma rays through the soil to detectors in the gauge, and the detection rate is correlated to total unit weight of the soil. When not in use for testing, the nuclear source is protected inside of the shielded gauge. Procedures for using a nuclear gauge to measure unit weight and water content can be found in ASTM D6938. Proper, regular calibration of nuclear gauges is essential to obtain consistent and accurate results.

Guidelines for the safe operation and licensing are provided by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) in NUREG/BR-0133, Working Safely with Nuclear Gauges (NRC 1996). Technicians working with nuclear gauges should be trained in the safe operation and handling of the gauge. They also need to wear a dosimeter that is periodically tested to confirm no unexpected exposure, although the risks are relatively minor due to the low energy emitted and the safety precautions built into the gauge.
key_points: Nuclear gauge (ASTM D6938) uses gamma rays from Cesium-231 source correlated to total unit weight; moisture measured by neutron backscatter.
Regular calibration is essential for consistent and accurate results.
NRC licensing and safety requirements apply per NUREG/BR-0133; operators must be trained and wear dosimeters.
Radiation risk is relatively minor due to low energy output and built-in safety features.
sections.applicability: Applies when using nuclear gauge technology to measure in situ soil unit weight and moisture content during compaction quality control.

sections.title: Non-nuclear Gauge Methods
sections.summary: Summarizes alternative non-nuclear technologies for assessing as-compacted soil density, developed to avoid NRC licensing requirements. Table 2-20 compares five device types (M-DI, EDG, SDG, license-exempt gauge, and stiffness-based devices) based on field performance evaluations by Berney et al. (2013, 2016). Notes that stiffness-based devices do not directly provide unit weight or moisture content.
sections.body: Because of the NRC requirements regarding licensing and transportation of nuclear gauges, several agencies (including the U.S. military) have been researching reliable alternatives to the nuclear gauge. Interestingly, these groups are also assessing direct measurement of the in situ strength and/or stiffness to replace the traditional density-moisture content specification for compacted soil. Table 2-20 provides a summary of various techniques and their performance compared to the "traditional" nuclear gauge based on field assessments by Berney et al. (2013, 2016). These devices are commercially available and operate using different principles.
key_points: Non-nuclear alternatives developed to avoid NRC licensing and transportation requirements.
Five device categories: M-DI (TDR), EDG (high RF), SDG (EIS), license-exempt gauge (Cs-127), and stiffness-based devices (LFD, DCP, IST, SS).
License-exempt soil density gauge (Cs-127) shows highest correlation to traditional nuclear gauge results.
EDG has highest precision but requires extensive site-specific soil calibration.
Stiffness-based devices (DCP, LFD, IST, SS) do not directly provide unit weight or moisture content.
Field performance data from Berney et al. (2013, 2016) presented in Table 2-20.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting non-nuclear alternatives to measure as-compacted soil density, particularly when NRC licensing or transportation of nuclear gauges is restricted.

sections.title: Measurement of As-Compacted Soil Moisture Content
sections.summary: Describes gravimetric and indirect methods for field measurement of as-compacted soil moisture content. Gravimetric methods (Table 2-21) physically dry the soil; indirect methods (Table 2-22) correlate moisture to surrogate parameters such as gas pressure or dielectric constant. Table 2-23 provides a statistical comparison of bias, accuracy, and precision for ten methods relative to the laboratory oven standard (ASTM D2216).
sections.body:
The standard method to measure moisture content is the laboratory oven and is the appropriate basis of comparison for all other methods. Unfortunately, drying in the oven requires a 24-hour time period at a temperature of 110°C ± 5°C (ASTM D2216), which is too slow for quality control of engineered fill. At least ten alternative methods have been developed for in situ moisture content evaluation. These methods can be classified either as: (1) gravimetric, in which the soil is actually heated and dried; or (2) indirect, in which the moisture content is correlated to another parameter, as the soil is not physically dried.

Gravimetric methods for field measurement of moisture content are compared to ASTM D2216 in Table 2-21. In all four cases, the soil is physically dried to obtain total mass and dry mass measurements from which moisture content is calculated.

A number of indirect methods have been developed to assess moisture content without physically drying the soil. As summarized in Table 2-22, these methods use a surrogate for temperature (i.e., gas pressure, dielectric constant changes, electrical impedance, etc.). Moisture content has a benchmark test that can and should be used - the laboratory oven. Each method has specific advantages and disadvantages, which can be expressed in statistical terms of bias, accuracy, and precision. Table 2-23 summarizes a comparison of the techniques (Berney et al. 2012, 2013).
key_points: Laboratory oven (ASTM D2216, 110°C for 24 hr) is the standard reference method for moisture content.
Two classification categories: gravimetric (physical drying) and indirect (surrogate parameter correlation).
Gravimetric field methods include standard microwave (ASTM D4643), field microwave, direct heating (ASTM D4959), and moisture analyzer (Table 2-21).
Indirect methods include nuclear density gauge (ASTM D6938), EDG (ASTM D7698), SDG, gas pressure tester (ASTM D4944/Speedy), and electromagnetic gauge (Table 2-22).
Table 2-23 shows statistical bias, accuracy (R²), and precision (std. dev.) for all ten methods relative to lab oven.
Gas pressure tester (Speedy) has highest bias (1.405); moisture analyzer has lowest precision standard deviation (0.044).
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting and evaluating methods for rapid or field measurement of as-compacted soil moisture content during earthwork quality control.

sections.title: Rock Properties
sections.summary: Introduces in situ testing methods for rock, explaining that while laboratory core tests reflect intact rock properties, engineering performance in the field is governed by rock discontinuities. Lists six in situ tests covered: plate load, flat jack, rock dilatometer, rock borehole shear, field direct shear, and rock joint hydraulic conductivity. Notes specialized nature and cost typically requires specialty contractors.
sections.body: Strength and stiffness tests on rock core tend to reflect the characteristics of the "intact" rock, while the engineering performance of rock in the field is governed by the rock discontinuities (Deere and Deere 1988; Bieniawski 1989). Therefore, in situ tests that include rock discontinuities and assess their impact are useful. The following tests are discussed in this section: plate load, flat jack, rock dilatometer, rock borehole shear, field direct shear, and rock joint hydraulic conductivity. Because of the specialized nature of this testing and the cost of the equipment, many of these in situ testing methods for rock are subcontracted to a specialty contractor.
key_points: Laboratory core tests reflect intact rock properties; field performance is governed by discontinuities.
In situ tests that capture discontinuity effects are essential for accurate rock engineering assessments.
Six in situ rock tests covered: plate load, flat jack, rock dilatometer, rock borehole shear, field direct shear, and hydraulic conductivity of joints.
Specialized equipment and expertise usually requires subcontracting to specialty contractors.
sections.applicability: Applies when planning or selecting in situ testing methods for evaluating rock mass strength, stiffness, and hydraulic conductivity at a project site.

sections.title: Strength and Stiffness Tests on Rock Masses
sections.summary: Covers five in situ methods for evaluating rock mass stiffness and strength: plate load test (ASTM D4394/D4395), flat jack test (ASTM D4729), rock dilatometer (similar to PMT per ASTM D4719), borehole jack (Goodman jack, ASTM D4971), and rock borehole shear test. Describes principles, equipment, applicable rock types, and references for each method.
sections.body:
Plate load testing (ASTM D4394, D4395) on rock is an in situ test method that evaluates the rock mass stiffness (Goodman 1989, George et al. 1999). The test can also assess the strength of medium to low strength rock. The results from rock plate load tests are presented in terms of stress vs. displacement. Tests often include a series of loading and unloading cycles to help isolate the influence of fractures and discontinuities. Generally, the results are analyzed using solutions based on elastic theory to calculate an equivalent modulus, Eʹ (Hoek 2007, Goodman 1989).

The plate bearing test requires a large reaction system to apply the required force. As an alternative, the flat jack concept uses a relatively thin (i.e., ~0.25 inches thick), flat, hydraulic jack that is inserted into a slot in the rock, thus allowing the rock to provide its own reaction. The flat jack test (ASTM D4729) is performed to assess the in situ state of stress in the rock and the rock mass stiffness.

For a geotechnical engineer who is familiar with in situ soil testing, a rock dilatometer is a misnomer, because it is actually a high-capacity pressuremeter (see Section 2-9.1.1). Operating procedures for a rock dilatometer are generally similar to those identified in ASTM D4719. The rock dilatometer test involves placing a long, cylindrical probe into a rock corehole and inflating a membrane on the probe. The membrane is expanded laterally while measuring the radial deformation. The results are used to evaluate rock mass stiffness.

The rock dilatometer may not be able to sufficiently stress the rock without rupturing the membrane. The borehole jack, commonly called a Goodman jack, overcomes this problem using small internal hydraulic jacks to induce lateral force across opposing curved steel platens that each stress a 90° sector of the borehole wall over a length of 8 inches. Equipment description and operating procedures are presented in ASTM D4971. The borehole jack can be used in boreholes cored with NX-size coring equipment. The hydraulic system used for the borehole jack can generate up to 10,000 psi, so it can be used on virtually any rock. The borehole jack is a common in situ rock test that does not require extensive experience to perform and obtain reliable results.

The rock borehole shear test is an alternative in situ borehole method for relatively weak rock or rock that is easily disturbed upon drilling and coring (e.g., weathered rock, fractured rock, shale, etc.). This test is a modification of the Iowa borehole shear test originally developed for soil (Yang et al. 2006). The rock borehole shear test measures the shear strength of rock. While there is no recognized testing standard, guidelines for the rock borehole shear test are presented in Lutenegger and Hallberg (1981). The device is lowered down the hole to the desired test elevation. Hydraulic pressure is applied to shear plates to obtain the desired normal stress, and a tether is pulled to create a shear force on the plates. The normal stress and shear stress are recorded. The calculated shear stress values for each of three or four normal stresses provide the data points to construct a strength envelope.
key_points: Rock plate load test (ASTM D4394/D4395) measures rock mass stiffness and strength; results analyzed via elastic theory to compute equivalent modulus E'.
Flat jack test (ASTM D4729) uses rock's own reaction; assesses in situ stress state and rock mass stiffness.
Rock dilatometer is a high-capacity pressuremeter (ASTM D4719) used in coreholesto measure radial deformation and evaluate rock mass stiffness.
Goodman jack (ASTM D4971) overcomes dilatometer membrane rupture limitation; operates up to 10,000 psi in NX-size boreholes.
Rock borehole shear test applies multiple normal stresses to construct a strength envelope; no recognized standard but guidelines per Lutenegger & Hallberg (1981).
Borehole jack is accessible to non-specialists; rock borehole shear test suited for weak or easily disturbed rock.
sections.applicability: Applies when in situ evaluation of rock mass stiffness and shear strength is needed, especially where discontinuities govern engineering performance.

sections.title: Direct Shear Tests on Rock Discontinuities
sections.summary: Describes large-scale in situ direct shear testing of rock discontinuities (ASTM D4554), performed on natural outcrops, in tunnels, or excavations. Covers the range of discontinuity types (clean fractures to clay-filled joints), test setup using a confining ring and plaster of Paris encasement, and interpretation to obtain peak and residual shear strength parameters from normal-shear stress failure envelopes.
sections.body:
Rock mass behavior governs the engineering performance, as dictated by discontinuities, which can vary from clean fractures with a certain surface roughness caused by asperities to weathered rock joints to clay-filled fractures. Many field applications load those discontinuities in shear (e.g., rock slopes, tunnel side walls and crown). Undisturbed, representative samples of discontinuities can be difficult to obtain.

Direct shear testing of rock discontinuities has been developed similar to direct shear testing for soils. The test equipment is highly specialized and quite large. Large-scale in situ direct shear tests on rock are performed on rock exposed from natural rock outcrops, in tunnels, or in excavations. In almost all cases, the test is performed to evaluate the strength of the discontinuity.

A description and discussion of the use of large-scale direct shear testing of rock by USACE is presented in Zeigler (1972). Standardized testing procedures are presented in ASTM D4554. A confining ring is placed around the in situ rock specimen such that the discontinuity is parallel to the ring. The specimen is encased in the ring using plaster of Paris or hydrostone. Normal and shear loads are applied perpendicular and parallel to the discontinuity, and displacements are measured.

While the performance of large-scale in situ direct shear tests on rock discontinuities can be daunting and difficult, the interpretation is similar to the conventional direct shear test performed on soil specimens. Pairs of normal and shear stress are plotted to define the failure envelope and shear strength parameters. In rock and along rock discontinuities, it is possible to measure the peak and residual strength of the discontinuities (Goodman 1970).
key_points: In situ direct shear tests (ASTM D4554) performed on natural outcrops, in tunnels, or excavations to evaluate discontinuity shear strength.
Discontinuities range from clean rough fractures to weathered joints to clay-filled fractures.
Specimen encased in confining ring with plaster of Paris/hydrostone; loads applied perpendicular and parallel to discontinuity.
Interpretation same as conventional direct shear: pairs of normal and shear stress define the failure envelope.
Both peak and residual shear strength can be measured for rock discontinuities.
Undisturbed representative samples of rock discontinuities are difficult to obtain, making in situ testing essential.
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating shear strength of rock discontinuities for designs involving rock slopes, tunnels, or excavations where discontinuities govern behavior.

sections.title: Hydraulic Conductivity of Rock Discontinuities
sections.summary: Describes the lugeon test using a five-step double packer method to quantify water flow in jointed rock. Defines the lugeon unit (~1×10⁻⁵ cm/s for laminar flow) and presents five flow behavior groups (laminar, turbulent, dilation, wash-out, void filling). Table 2-24 provides lugeon value classifications, approximate hydraulic conductivities, and discontinuity conditions used to select grouting strategies for hydraulic barriers.
sections.body:
Water flows through rocks occurs mostly in open voids, fractures, joints, and other discontinuities, which contribute to the "primary" porosity of the rock. Water flow in this regime may be turbulent instead of laminar and may not be governed by Darcy's law, making quantification of water flow in rock discontinuities challenging. In the 1930s, the lugeon was introduced to quantify water flow in jointed rock (Houlsby 1976). A lugeon is defined as the flow of one liter of water per meter per minute under a pressure of 10 bars (145 psi) in a constant head double packer test. For this situation, a lugeon is approximately 1×10⁻⁵ cm/s for laminar flow conditions.

To assess the flow regime for water in rock joints, the five-step test method summarized in Figure 2-23 was developed. Based on the five-step test results, the rock is characterized as being in one of five groups (Houlsby 1976):

• Group A – Laminar Flow: Lugeon values relatively constant through all five steps
• Group B – Turbulent: Lowest lugeon occurs at highest pressure
• Group C – Dilation: Highest lugeon occurs at highest pressure
• Group D – Wash-out: Lugeon increases as test progresses
• Group E – Void Filing: Lugeon decreases as test progresses

These characterizations are commonly used to select the appropriate grouting strategy for hydraulic barriers in jointed rock. The interpretation of the lugeon test and physical characterization of the jointed rock is shown in Table 2-24.
key_points: Lugeon unit defined as 1 L/m/min at 10 bars (145 psi); approximately 1×10⁻⁵ cm/s for laminar flow.
Water flow in rock may be turbulent and not governed by Darcy's law.
Five-step double packer test identifies five flow behavior groups: laminar (A), turbulent (B), dilation (C), wash-out (D), void filling (E).
Lugeon test results used to select grouting strategies for hydraulic barriers in jointed rock.
Table 2-24 classifies lugeon values (<1 to >100) into Very Low to Very High conductivity with corresponding rock mass conditions.
Lugeon test developed in the 1930s; method refined by Houlsby (1976).
sections.applicability: Applies when characterizing hydraulic conductivity of jointed rock for dam foundations, hydraulic barriers, or grouting program design.

sections.title: Field Instrumentation and Monitoring
sections.summary: Introduces geotechnical field instrumentation as a critical practice for monitoring structural performance, forensic investigations, and early warning systems. Covers the purpose of monitoring, the range of instruments available, and key references including Dunnicliff (1993) and USACE manuals. Sets the framework for subsections on specific instrument types and field applications.
sections.body: Monitoring the performance of geotechnical structures is a vital consideration for individual projects and has helped guide the evolution of the practice (Peck 1969). Monitoring field performance starts with an assessment of what "performance" is anticipated. Once this is established, instruments may need to be installed before, during, and/or after construction or after a failure as part of the forensic investigation to understand the failure mechanisms. Finally, certain instruments may be integral components of early warning systems for sensitive structures. This section summarizes the types of geotechnical instrumentation and their operations to help guide the geotechnical engineer in selecting the most appropriate instrument for a given project. In-depth details regarding geotechnical instrumentation can be found in USACE (1987, 1995b), Bartholomew et al. (1987, 1987a), FHWA (1988) and most notably Dunnicliff (1993). The rapid evolution of the various measurement technologies and the recognition of the importance of performance monitoring will undoubtedly result in further expansion and utility of geotechnical instrumentation over the coming years.
key_points: Monitoring must begin with a clear definition of expected performance for the specific project.
Instruments may be needed before, during, and after construction, or post-failure for forensic investigations.
Certain instruments serve as integral components of early warning systems for sensitive structures.
Key references include Dunnicliff (1993), USACE (1987, 1995b), Bartholomew et al. (1987), and FHWA (1988).
Technology evolution is rapidly expanding the utility of geotechnical instrumentation.
sections.applicability: Applies to all geotechnical projects where field performance monitoring, forensic investigation, or early warning systems are required.

sections.title: Operating Concepts for Geotechnical Monitoring Instruments
sections.summary: Describes the major types of geotechnical monitoring transducers (mechanical, pneumatic, hydraulic, electrical, MEMS, fiber optic) and the measurements they enable, including deformation, pore pressure, earth pressure, load, temperature, and vibration. Explains key instrument selection criteria: range, accuracy, precision, and calibration requirements.
sections.body:
Making a measurement of engineering performance involves using some type of instrument or transducer for obtaining the measurement. The major types of instruments are summarized in Table 2-25. The transducers introduced in this table are incorporated into instruments that are used to make specific measurements. These measurements may include: (1) deformations (e.g., horizontal movement of a landslide, vertical settlement, tilt of retaining wall), (2) pore pressures in soil (e.g., excess pore pressure due to consolidation or static water levels in wells), (3) earth pressures (e.g., pressures acting on earth retaining structures), (4) loads (e.g., strut loads in braced excavations, anchor loads on tiebacks, vertical loads for plate load tests), (5) temperature (e.g., frost penetration, thermal-induced stress/deformation), and (6) vibration (e.g., geophysical testing, blast monitoring, seismic activity).

Regardless of the type, selection of monitoring instruments must consider the instrument range, accuracy, and precision as well as the required calibration procedures. Geotechnical instruments have a specific measurement range, which must encompass the values anticipated in the field application. Instruments also have a precision, which refers to the smallest recordable unit that can be measured. For example, a 1,000 lb. capacity load cell that records to the nearest 0.1 lb. has a precision of 0.01% of its full range or full scale. The accuracy of an instrument refers to the ability to obtain a correct and repeatable measurement of the desired quantity. Instruments with a large range are not always sufficiently accurate at values near the lower end of the range. Many instruments require calibration to convert the measured property into the desired engineering property. While typically provided by the manufacturer, the calibration should be confirmed and repeated on a regular basis.
key_points: Six primary measurement categories: deformation, pore pressure, earth pressure, load, temperature, and vibration.
Instrument types include mechanical, pneumatic, hydraulic, electrical, MEMS, and fiber optic transducers.
