Range must encompass anticipated field values; precision is the smallest recordable unit.
Accuracy refers to repeatability and correctness of measurement; large-range instruments may be inaccurate at low values.
Calibration, typically from the manufacturer, must be confirmed and repeated regularly.
Fiber optic sensors enable distributed strain measurement along the full length of a structure.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting any geotechnical monitoring instrument, to ensure the chosen transducer type meets the project's range, accuracy, precision, and calibration requirements.

sections.title: Linear Deformation Measurements
sections.summary: Covers the full spectrum of methods for monitoring linear deformation in geotechnical structures, from simple visual observation and crack pins to automated total stations, surface settlement plates, liquid level systems, and borehole extensometers. Emphasizes that simple methods should not be overlooked and explains operational details, accuracy, and limitations of each technique.
sections.body:
There are many applications where deformation monitoring is either imperative or, at least beneficial (see Section 2-10.9 below). The deformation could involve vertical movement from consolidation adjacent to a deep excavation, horizontal and rotational movements from a landslide, or outward tilt of a retaining wall. Methods for determining linear deformation are summarized in Table 2-26 and can range from simple to relatively complex.

Simple methods for deformation monitoring should not be overlooked. Peck (1972) notes that the human eye is too often overlooked and "can detect most of what we need to know about subsurface construction." Measurements by crack pins and tape measure can be used to monitor observed cracks in soils adjacent to slopes or cracks in rock. If conditions warrant, distances can be continuously monitored using a displacement transducer as shown in Figure 2-24. When considering instruments for monitoring observed cracks in the walls of buildings, a mechanical grid crack gauge can be monitored to show magnitude and direction of movement over time. This gauge is simply attached across the crack using epoxy or pins through the mounting holes.

Where needed, more precise deformation measurements can be made using transducers. When monitoring deformations over relatively short time periods or when the instrument is protected, a simple dial gauge may be used. For automated readings, an electrical transducer (i.e., linear variable displacement transformer (LVDT), direct current LVDT, or linear potentiometer) provides a precise and potentially highly accurate alternative.

Conventional field survey equipment can be used to monitor deformations of several points over large distances and often over long time periods, based on a common benchmark. Such surveys must be "closed" by shooting the benchmark before and after the survey. Automated total stations (AMTS) can provide accurate near real-time monitoring for multiple points and are especially useful for monitoring construction-induced movements. The accuracy of the AMTS is inversely proportional to the distance from instrument to prism (or object), but can be used at distances greater than 1,000 feet. As with any surveying option, it is always desired to include a benchmark point during each reading cycle. The AMTS uses a laser for finding and monitoring the target so it can be used day or night.

The magnitude and time-rate of consolidation settlements during construction are often used to direct certain construction activities (i.e., fill placement rate). Monitoring long-term settlement is often desired. Surface settlement plates (often referred to as platforms) are monitored using conventional surveying instruments and provide an accurate and relatively inexpensive technique. The settlement plate is placed on the original ground surface before fill placement commences. It is necessary to protect the pipe from being damaged or tilted during construction by either vehicle impact or differential fill placement around the riser pipe. As with all survey measurements, a non-moving benchmark is to be shot during each cycle of readings. More advanced systems use liquid pressure to measure change in height below a fixed reservoir or probes to measure the profile of settlement in a buried tube.
key_points: Visual observation (human eye) is a low-cost, often-overlooked method for detecting subsurface construction issues.
Crack pins, tape measures, and grid crack gauges are simple, effective tools for monitoring cracks in soil, rock, and structures.
LVDTs and dial gauges provide precise automated or manual deformation readings over short durations.
Automated Total Stations (AMTS) enable near real-time, multi-point monitoring; accuracy is inversely proportional to distance.
Field surveys must be 'closed' by referencing a benchmark before and after each survey.
Surface settlement plates are accurate and inexpensive; riser pipes must be protected during construction.
Liquid level settlement gauges and profilers offer distributed settlement measurements without riser pipes, at higher initial cost.
Borehole extensometers measure relative displacement at multiple depths along a borehole axis.
sections.applicability: Applies when monitoring vertical settlement, horizontal movement, or crack deformation in geotechnical structures such as embankments, slopes, retaining walls, and areas near deep excavations.

sections.title: Angular Displacement Measurements
sections.summary: Describes instruments for measuring angular displacement and tilt in geotechnical applications, including tiltmeters, slope inclinometers, and in-place inclinometers. Explains their operating principles, typical applications (landslides, retaining walls, deep excavations), and key limitations such as casing damage from excessive deformation and the need for bias correction in data processing.
sections.body: Angular displacement measurements are used to measure relative displacements of slopes or tilting of structures, such as retaining walls. These instruments can be used to determine the location of planes of sliding and to give warnings when structures become out-of-vertical. Types of angular displacement instruments are summarized in Table 2-27.
key_points: Angular displacement instruments identify sliding planes and provide warnings of structural out-of-vertical conditions.
Tiltmeters use accelerometers to measure inclination; MEMS tiltmeters can achieve range up to 40 arc minutes and precision of 1 arc second.
Slope inclinometers use grooved casing grouted into a borehole with a biaxial accelerometer probe pulled through at regular intervals.
Two passes through inclinometer casing are required for quality data; bias correction must be applied during processing.
Excessive deformation can prevent ongoing use of inclinometer casing.
In-place inclinometers remain fixed in the casing, can be automated, and MEMS versions do not require special casing.
sections.applicability: Applies when measuring tilt of retaining walls, locating slip planes in landslides, or monitoring lateral deformation around deep excavations.

sections.title: Pore Pressure and Water Pressure Measurements
sections.summary: Covers piezometer types used to measure transient and static pore water pressures, including pneumatic, hydraulic (twin-tube), electrical, and MEMS devices. Explains hydrodynamic lag time and its significance for instrument selection — particularly that open standpipe wells are unsuitable for transient pore pressure measurement in low-permeability soils.
sections.body:
Transducers that are capable of measuring transient water pressures are commonly relied upon for pore pressure measurements. These transducers are often generically referenced as piezometers. This is in contrast to the use of the term standpipe piezometer in Section 2-8 to describe a specific type of well. As described above, the same basic technology can be used for measuring both static and transient water pressures, and the transducer types include pneumatic, hydraulic, electrical, and MEMS devices. Operation and application of these piezometers are summarized in Table 2-28. All of these methods measure positive water pressures in saturated soil.

Hydrodynamic lag time or simply lag time refers to the time required for an instrument to respond to a change in pressure. Figure 2-31 plots the estimated lag time (in terms of time for 90% response) for various types of wells and piezometers compared to the hydraulic conductivity of the soil. Note the short lag time for diaphragm transducers and the extended time lag for open piezometer wells. As indicated by the figure, open wells cannot effectively measure hydrodynamic water pressures for transient flow situations.
key_points: Piezometers measure transient and static water pressures in saturated soil; four main types: pneumatic, hydraulic, electrical, and MEMS.
Pneumatic piezometers do not require a power source, are insensitive to stray electrical signals, and suit long-term monitoring.
Electrical and MEMS diaphragm piezometers have very short lag times and can be automated and remotely monitored.
MEMS sensors experience electrical drift; recalibration is possible if the sensor remains accessible.
Hydrodynamic lag time is the time for 90% instrument response to a pressure change; critical for transient measurement.
Open standpipe wells have long lag times and cannot effectively measure hydrodynamic pressures in transient flow situations.
Electrical/MEMS diaphragm piezometers require very little water flow to move the diaphragm, enabling rapid response.
sections.applicability: Applies when measuring pore water pressures in saturated soil, especially during transient flow conditions such as consolidation, embankment loading, or drawdown events.

sections.title: Earth Pressure Measurements
sections.summary: Discusses the use of earth pressure cells (total stress cells) and tactile pressure sensors to measure in-situ vertical and horizontal stresses. Covers operating principles, installation requirements (cell size, thickness-to-diameter ratio, bedding with fine sand), and the challenge of stress arching around the cell. References Filz and Brandon (1994) and Sehn (1990) for installation guidance.
sections.body:
Although uncommon, measurement of the actual vertical and/or horizontal stress in the ground is sometimes desired. The concept for making these measurements is easy, while the interpretation of the results can be challenging. An earth pressure cell (a.k.a., total stress cell) measures stress by deformations of a thin diaphragm or transfer of pressure to a hydraulic cell. Deformations of the diaphragm-type cell can be measured by a strain gauge, vibrating wire transducer, or MEMS gauge. Earth pressure cells make an internal measurement compared with most of other transducers that monitor soil response externally. The presence of the cell alters the stresses in the soil due to differences between the stiffness of the cell and the soil. Good summaries of the influence of installation and type of earth pressure cells can be found in Filz and Brandon (1994) and Sehn (1990). As an alternative to earth pressure cells, tactile pressure sensors are thin, flexible polymer sheets with many embedded strain sensors that allow stress to be measured (Paikowsky et al. 2006).

From experience, earth pressure cells should be relatively large (i.e., 9 to 12 inches) in diameter and thin, resulting in a ratio of thickness to diameter of less than 1:10. The cell must be in intimate contact with the soil and is generally surrounded (i.e., bedded) using fine sand to minimize potential for stress concentrations from large particles in the soil.
key_points: Earth pressure cells measure total stress via diaphragm deformation or hydraulic pressure transfer.
The presence of the cell alters local stresses due to stiffness differences between cell and soil — interpretation is challenging.
Recommended cell dimensions: 9–12 inches diameter, thickness-to-diameter ratio less than 1:10.
Cells must be bedded in fine sand to ensure intimate contact and minimize stress concentrations.
Tactile pressure sensors (flexible polymer sheets with embedded strain gauges) are an alternative for distributed stress measurement.
Key references for installation guidance: Filz and Brandon (1994), Sehn (1990).
sections.applicability: Applies when direct measurement of vertical or horizontal in-situ stress is needed, such as for earth retaining structures, embankment dams, or forensic investigations.

sections.title: Load Measurements
sections.summary: Summarizes common load-measuring instruments used in geotechnical projects, including hydraulic load cells, calibrated hydraulic jacks (e.g., Osterberg O-Cell), electric load cells, and embedded/surface-mounted strain gauges. Table 2-29 provides operational details, accuracy ranges, and comments on each instrument type.
sections.body: Many applications in geotechnical projects require the measurement of load. A summary of the common load measuring instruments is provided in Table 2-29.
key_points: Hydraulic load cells measure load via internal pressure increase; capable of >500 tons capacity at ~0.1% accuracy; no external power needed with mechanical transducer.
Calibrated hydraulic jacks (e.g., Osterberg O-Cell) are used for drilled shaft load testing; same advantages as hydraulic load cells.
Electric load cells use bonded strain gauges or vibrating wire transducers; wide range of sizes and capacities; require external power.
Embedded and surface-mounted strain gauges measure strain in structural members; must be correctly located and protected during construction.
Sister bar gauges can be pre-attached and welded to reinforcing cages for embedded measurement.
sections.applicability: Applies when measuring loads in geotechnical structures such as braced excavation struts, tieback anchors, drilled shafts, or driven piles.

sections.title: Temperature Measurements
sections.summary: Describes three categories of temperature measurement in geotechnical engineering: direct temperature measurement (e.g., frost penetration), measurement of temperatures that induce structural loads (e.g., strut thermal expansion), and measurement of temperatures affecting transducer performance (e.g., viscosity changes in hydraulic systems). Thermocouples, RTDs, and thermistors are the primary instruments.
sections.body:
As described in Dunnicliff (1993), temperature measurements in geotechnical engineering are typically obtained for one of three specific reasons. The appropriate instrument for the specific application should be selected and used accordingly.

• Direct Measurement: Temperature measurements may be required for projects, such as depth of frost penetration, soil temperature beneath industrial furnaces, temperatures of thermal piles. Thermocouples and resistance temperature devices (RTDs) are the most common devices for these applications.

• Measurement of Temperatures that Induce Loads: Temperature changes cause thermal expansion and contraction of materials. The loads in structural members (e.g., struts for excavation support, tunnel support systems) will be impacted when subjected to temperature fluctuations. Again, thermocouple or RTDs are commonly used for these applications.

• Measurement of Temperatures that Influence Transducer Performance: Transducer temperatures can also have significant impacts on the response of geotechnical instruments themselves. For example, in closed hydraulic systems, temperature can change the viscosity of the fluid and can cause expansion and/or contraction of the fluid and the hoses. These changes will influence the interpreted response unless appropriate corrections are made. Instrument manufacturers will report the necessary corrections. Monitoring temperature changes for transducers requires accurate measurement of small temperature changes. The thermistors used for this purpose are usually built directly into the transducer by the manufacturer.
key_points: Three reasons for temperature measurement: direct temperature needs, thermally-induced loads, and transducer performance correction.
Thermocouples and RTDs are standard for direct temperature and load-inducing temperature measurement.
Temperature affects closed hydraulic system viscosity and fluid/hose expansion, altering instrument readings if uncorrected.
Thermistors for transducer temperature correction are typically built into the instrument by the manufacturer.
Manufacturer-reported correction factors must be applied to account for temperature effects on transducer performance.
sections.applicability: Applies when geotechnical projects involve frost penetration monitoring, thermally-induced structural loads, or when temperature corrections to transducer readings are required.

sections.title: Vibration Measurements
sections.summary: Describes steady-state and transient vibration monitoring in geotechnical applications. Steady-state vibrations from machinery are assessed with MEMS accelerometers or handheld meters. Transient vibrations from pile driving, blasting, or seismic activity require portable seismographs with geophones or accelerometers, high sampling rates, and threshold-triggered recording with pre-event capture capability.
sections.body:
In some specialty cases, the measurement of vibrations may be a component of a performance monitoring program. Both steady state vibrations and transient vibrations may be of interest.

• Steady State Vibrations: Oscillating machinery that can induce vibratory loads to the foundation and foundation soils. These vibrations may induce cracks in concrete floors, walls, masonry, or finishes. Vibration transducers use accelerometers (often MEMS based) to assess the magnitude and frequency of the vibration. These transducers may be included in portable handheld meters that are effective at capturing the induced vibrations from the machinery. Modern smartphones use MEMS accelerometers and can be used to assess vibrations.

• Transient Vibrations: Transient vibrations may be induced by construction activity, such as equipment traffic, pile driving, dynamic compaction, or blasting; machinery; or seismic activity. Transient vibration monitoring is an integral part of many of the geophysical tests discussed in Section 2-4. Transient vibrations are captured by accelerometers and require high sampling rates in order to capture vibrations that may occur over a few seconds. Of particular interest for the transient vibrations are the magnitude, duration, and frequency content.

Capturing and storing vibration data for detailed analysis usually requires dedicated hardware, specifically portable (or permanent) seismographs. This equipment may include geophones to measure ground velocity or accelerometers to measure ground acceleration. The equipment usually has a user-defined threshold limit for the device to trigger its recording and the ability to capture data a few seconds before the triggering event. A brief discussion of the equipment to measure and capture ground vibrations is presented in NCHRP (2018). There are engineering firms that specialize in measuring transient vibrations.
key_points: Steady-state vibrations from machinery are assessed using MEMS accelerometers; modern smartphones can also be used.
Transient vibrations (pile driving, blasting, seismic) require high sampling rates and are of interest for magnitude, duration, and frequency content.
Seismographs with geophones (velocity) or accelerometers (acceleration) are standard for transient vibration capture.
User-defined threshold triggers and pre-event data capture are key seismograph features for transient monitoring.
Transient vibration monitoring is integral to geophysical testing (see Section 2-4).
Specialized engineering firms are available for transient vibration measurement programs.
sections.applicability: Applies when monitoring vibrations from oscillating machinery, construction activities (pile driving, blasting, dynamic compaction), or seismic events that may affect geotechnical structures or adjacent buildings.

sections.title: Field Applications for Instrumentation
sections.summary: Provides a framework for selecting geotechnical instrumentation based on specific performance questions, opposing the 'monitor everything' philosophy. Table 2-30 lists example performance questions for eleven project categories including braced excavations, embankment dams, driven piles, drilled shafts, dewatering, grouting, ground improvement, and liability control.
sections.body: Every instrument used to monitor geotechnical projects should be selected to answer a particular performance question. This approach opposes the tendency to adopt a philosophy of "if you can monitor it, you should monitor it," which is not recommended. Table 2-30 provides example performance questions that might be appropriate for various project types. Significant forethought should be given before an instrumentation plan is developed and the program should be organized around addressing specific questions. Additional discussion on these topics is provided in Dunnicliff (1993) and NCHRP (2018).
key_points: Each instrument must be selected to answer a specific, pre-defined performance question — not for general monitoring coverage.
The 'monitor everything' philosophy is explicitly not recommended.
Instrumentation plans should be developed with significant forethought and organized around specific questions.

Table 2-30 provides example performance questions for 11 project types: braced excavations, embankments on soft ground, embankment dams, slopes, underground construction, driven piles, drilled shafts, earth retaining structures, dewatering, grouting, ground improvement, and liability control.
Key references for instrumentation planning: Dunnicliff (1993) and NCHRP (2018).
sections.applicability: Applies when developing a geotechnical instrumentation and monitoring plan for any project type, to ensure instruments are selected purposefully to answer defined performance questions.

Each reference is linked to its specific topic area for quick lookup by practicing engineers.

sections.title: NOTATION
sections.summary: Defines all symbols and abbreviations used in Chapter 2, covering parameters from vane shear testing (VST), dilatometer testing (DMT), pressuremeter testing (PMT), and cone penetration testing (CPT). Includes mechanical parameters such as shear modulus, undrained shear strength, moduli, stress indices, and pressures specific to each in situ test method.
sections.body:
Symbol | Description
D | Diameter of the vane - VST
ED | Dilatometer modulus - DMT
Ep | Pressuremeter modulus - PMT
Eʹ | Equivalent modulus
fs | Sleeve friction - CPT
G | Shear modulus
ID | Material index
KD | Horizontal stress index - DMT
K0 | Coefficient of lateral earth pressure at rest
ks | Modulus of subgrade reaction
qt | Normalized tip resistance - CPT
qu | Tip resistance - CPT
RQD | Rock Quality Designation
St,fv | Sensitivity in undrained shear strength from vane shear test
su | Undrained shear strength
su,fv | Undrained shear strength from vane shear test
sur,fv | Remolded undrained shear strength from vane shear test
Tmax | Maximum net torque for vane shear test
Tres | Residual torque for vane shear test
V0 | Initial calculated volume within the uninflated membrane in PMT
µR | Vane correction factor
pf | Inflection point assumed to delineate the change from pseudo elastic to plastic response and the point where creep may be expected in PMT
p0 | Pressure at which recompression of disturbed soil in the side of the borehole is complete and expansion into undisturbed soil starts in PMT, also referred to as liftoff pressure
pr | Yield point during the reloading portion of a PMT unload–reload cycle where recompression ends and the soil reinitiates plastic shearing
pt | Limit pressure in PMT where the curve becomes asymptotic on a pressure versus volume curve
pu | Minimum pressure during unloading during the PMT unload–reload cycle
σh0 | Total horizontal stress
key_points: CPT parameters defined: sleeve friction (fs), normalized tip resistance (qt), and tip resistance (qu).
DMT parameters defined: dilatometer modulus (ED), horizontal stress index (KD), and material index (ID).
PMT parameters defined: modulus (Ep), liftoff pressure (p0), limit pressure (pt), inflection point (pf), yield point (pr), minimum unloading pressure (pu), and initial volume (V0).

VST parameters defined: vane diameter (D), maximum torque (Tmax), residual torque (Tres), undrained shear strength (su,fv), remolded strength (sur,fv), sensitivity (St,fv), and correction factor (µR).

General soil parameters include undrained shear strength (su), shear modulus (G), lateral earth pressure coefficient at rest (K0), modulus of subgrade reaction (ks), equivalent modulus (Eʹ), and total horizontal stress (σh0).
RQD (Rock Quality Designation) is included as a rock characterization parameter.
sections.applicability: Applies whenever interpreting symbols used anywhere in Chapter 2 of UFC 3-220-10, particularly for in situ test result calculations involving CPT, DMT, PMT, and VST methods.
